title: Security
audience: Has built or worked on a web application or an API
Wants to recognise and prevent the common security flaws in their own code

outcomes.description: Name what a system protects, mark its trust boundaries, and list threats to a feature with STRIDE.
Validate input at the boundary with allowlists, and say why it must also be made safe where it is used.
Recognise injection in SQL and shell commands, and prevent it by keeping code and data apart.
Explain how cross-site scripting happens, and prevent it with output encoding for the right context.
Describe how logins are attacked, and design login, MFA and password reset flows that resist it.
Store passwords with a salted, slow hash, and migrate an old scheme without a mass reset.
Choose between server-side sessions and tokens, protect the credential, and end a session properly.
Explain cross-site request forgery and the same-origin policy, and say what CORS does and does not do.
Find missing access checks, and structure authorization so that a forgotten check means no access.
Choose between hashing, a MAC, encryption and a signature for a need, and avoid the common misuse of each.
Keep secrets out of code, store and rotate them properly, and respond in the right order when one leaks.
Manage the risk of third-party code with scanning, pinning and updates, and protect the build pipeline.
Classify data, hold less of it for less time, and find where sensitive data ends up by accident.
Decide what to log and alert on, and follow the stages of incident response in the right order.
Review an application and a change for security flaws, and design a feature securely, without help.

lessons.title: Think like a defender
lessons.intro:
Security is the work of keeping a system doing what it should for the people it should, when someone is trying to make it do otherwise. This module gives you the vocabulary and one method for finding what could go wrong before an attacker does.

The advice in this course is general guidance for learning. It is not any organization's policy. Where you work, the security team's rules come first.

steps.title: What is being protected
steps.text:
Security has three goals, known together as the **CIA triad**.

| Goal | Means | Broken when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confidentiality | Only the right people can read the data | Customer records are leaked |
| Integrity | Only the right people can change the data, and changes are correct | An order's price is altered |
| Availability | The system works when it is needed | The site is knocked offline |

Most people think of confidentiality first. The other two matter as much. A bank whose balances can be edited has a worse problem than one whose balances can be read.

Start any security discussion by naming the **assets**: the things worth protecting. They are usually data (personal details, payment data, credentials), money, and the ability to act as someone (an account, an admin role, a signing key).

steps.title: Threats, vulnerabilities and risk
steps.text:
Three words are often mixed up.

- A **threat** is something bad that could happen: someone reads another user's messages.
- A **vulnerability** is a weakness that makes it possible: the messages endpoint does not check who is asking.
- **Risk** is how much the two matter together: how likely it is, multiplied by how bad it would be.

Risk is what you manage. You cannot remove every vulnerability, and you do not need to. A weakness in an internal tool that holds no sensitive data matters less than the same weakness in the login page.

So security work is a matter of priorities. The question is never "is this perfectly secure". It is "what are the worst things that could happen here, and which ones have we left open".

steps.title: The attack surface
steps.text:
The **attack surface** is every place where someone outside can send input to the system or get output from it.

- Every URL and API endpoint, including old and undocumented ones.
- Every form field, header, cookie, query parameter and uploaded file.
- Admin panels, debug pages and status endpoints.
- Open ports, storage buckets, message queues.
- The people who can be tricked, and the dependencies you install.

A smaller surface is easier to defend. Removing an unused endpoint, closing a port or deleting a feature nobody uses is security work, and it is often the cheapest kind.

steps.title: Trust boundaries
steps.text:
A **trust boundary** is a line where data passes from something you do not control to something you do. The clearest one is between a user's browser and your server.

The rule at every boundary is the same: data that crosses it is untrusted until your side has checked it.

Many security bugs come from a wrong belief about where the boundary lies. The browser is on the far side. That includes everything your own JavaScript does there. A check that runs in the browser, a hidden form field, a disabled button, a price stored in the page: the user controls all of these. They can be changed with tools built into every browser.

steps.title: Checked in the wrong place
steps.text: A shop's checkout page computes the order total in the browser and sends it to the server in a field named `total`. The server charges the card that amount.

steps.title: Who attacks, and why
steps.text:
It helps to picture who you are defending against. Their effort and skill differ a great deal.

- **Automated scanners.** Programs that try every address on the internet for known weaknesses. They find anything exposed within hours. Most real attacks start here.
- **Opportunists.** People using published tools and leaked password lists. They go where it is easy.
- **Targeted attackers.** People who want your system in particular and will spend time on it.
- **Insiders.** People with legitimate access who misuse it, or whose accounts are taken over.
- **Users who make mistakes.** Not attackers at all. A system should not let an honest mistake cause a breach.

The first two account for most incidents, and they are stopped by basics: updated software, strong authentication, checked input and nothing exposed that need not be.

steps.title: Principles that hold everywhere
steps.text:
A few ideas apply to every later module.

- **Least privilege.** Give each user, service and key only the access it needs. A stolen key can then do only what that key could do.
- **Defence in depth.** Use several independent layers, so that one mistake is not a breach. Validation, a parameterised query and a database account with limited rights each stop SQL injection on their own.
- **Deny by default.** Start with nothing allowed and add what is needed. A new endpoint that someone forgot to configure is then closed, not open.
- **Fail closed.** When a check cannot be completed, refuse. A permission service that is down should mean "no access", not "everyone in".
- **Keep it simple.** Complex systems hide mistakes. The more that can be understood at a glance, the fewer surprises.
- **Do not rely on secrecy of the design.** Assume an attacker knows how the system works. Security must come from keys and checks, not from nobody knowing the URL.

steps.title: Threat modelling
steps.text:
**Threat modelling** is a structured way of asking what could go wrong, done before or while building. Four questions are enough.

1. **What are we building?** Draw the parts and the data flowing between them. Mark the trust boundaries.
2. **What can go wrong?** Go through each part and each arrow.
3. **What will we do about it?** Fix it, reduce it, or accept it knowingly.
4. **Did we do a good job?** Check afterwards.

For the second question, a list of prompts called **STRIDE** helps. Ask each of the six about every part.

| Letter | Threat | Question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S | Spoofing | Can someone pretend to be another user or service? |
| T | Tampering | Can someone change data they should not? |
| R | Repudiation | Could someone deny an action, with no record to show otherwise? |
| I | Information disclosure | Can someone read what they should not? |
| D | Denial of service | Can someone make it stop working? |
| E | Elevation of privilege | Can someone gain rights they were not given? |

A half-hour session with a whiteboard finds design flaws that no later code review will, because they are flaws in what was decided, not in how it was written.

steps.title: Fail open or closed
steps.text: A service checks permissions by calling a separate authorization service. The code is written so that if that call times out, the request is allowed, "to avoid an outage".

steps.title: Exercise: model a feature
steps.text:
A team adds "export my data" to a web application. A logged-in user clicks a button. The server builds a ZIP file of that user's records, stores it in a storage bucket, and emails the user a link to download it.

Draw the flow as a list of steps. Mark the trust boundaries. Then go through STRIDE and write at least one threat for each letter, with what you would do about it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Flow**

1. The browser sends "export" with the session cookie. (Boundary: browser to server.)
2. The server queues a job with the user's ID.
3. A worker reads that user's records and writes a ZIP to storage.
4. The server emails a link. (Boundary: the link leaves your system and travels by email.)
5. Someone opens the link and downloads the file. (Boundary: internet to storage.)

**Threats**

| | Threat | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S | Someone who takes over a session exports everything in one click | Ask for the password again, or a second factor, before a full export |
| T | The request names a user ID, and an attacker changes it to export another user's data | Take the user ID from the session on the server, never from the request |
| R | A user claims they never requested an export | Record who requested each export, when and from where |
| I | The download link works for anyone who has it, for ever | Make the link expire after a short time, make it unguessable, and require login to use it |
| D | Someone requests thousands of exports and fills storage or the job queue | Limit exports per user per day. Delete files after a few days |
| E | The worker's storage key can read and write every file in the bucket | Give the worker a key that can write only to the exports area |

The most serious are T and I. One lets an attacker choose whose data is exported. The other puts a whole account's data behind a link that sits in an email inbox. Both are design decisions, which is why they are cheapest to catch at this stage.

lessons.title: Treat all input as untrusted
lessons.intro:
Most attacks arrive as input: a value the system accepts and then uses in a way the sender chose. This module covers where input comes from, how to validate it, and why validation alone is never the whole defence.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: Everything from outside is input
steps.text:
Input is more than the fields of a form. It is every value that comes from the far side of a trust boundary.

- URL paths and query parameters.
- Request bodies: form fields, JSON, XML.
- Headers, including `User-Agent`, `Referer` and `X-Forwarded-For`.
- Cookies.
- Uploaded files: their content, their name and their declared type.
- Data from other systems: webhooks, API responses, imported files.
- Data read back from your own database, if a user put it there earlier.

The last item surprises people. A comment that a user stored yesterday is still user input today. It was untrusted when it arrived, and storing it did not make it safe.

A request that your own page generated is not safe either. Anyone can send a request by hand, with any values, without going near your page.

steps.title: Validation
steps.text:
**Validation** checks that input is what the system expects before the system uses it. Check on the server, at the boundary, on every request.

Check these, in this order.

1. **Type.** Is it a number, a date, a boolean, as required?
2. **Length and size.** Is it within sensible limits?
3. **Range.** Is the quantity between 1 and 100? Is the date in the future?
4. **Format.** Does it look like an email address, a postcode, an identifier?
5. **Membership.** Is it one of the allowed values?
6. **Business rules.** Does this user own this item? Is this combination allowed?

When validation fails, reject the request with a clear error. Do not try to repair bad input and carry on. Guessing what the sender meant is how filters get bypassed.

Checks in the browser are a convenience for honest users, who see an error without waiting for the server. They provide no security, since the sender can skip them.

steps.title: Allow what is good
steps.text:
There are two ways to write a check.

A **blocklist** names what is forbidden: reject input containing `<script>` or `DROP TABLE`. It fails, because there are endless ways to write a harmful value and the list never has all of them: different capitalisation, different encodings, a different tag.

An **allowlist** names what is permitted: a username is 3 to 30 letters, digits or underscores. Anything else is refused. It works because it describes the small set of good values and makes no attempt to list the bad ones.

Prefer an allowlist wherever the valid values can be described. For a value chosen from a list, such as a sort column, compare it against the list and use your own copy of the matching entry, never the text the user sent.

steps.title: Free text cannot be allowlisted
steps.text:
Some input has no narrow format: a name, a comment, an address. Names contain apostrophes, hyphens and letters from every alphabet. Rejecting `O'Brien` is a bug, not a defence.

For free text, validate what you can, which is length and the absence of control characters, and accept the rest. Then make it harmless at the place where it is used.

That is the second half of input handling, and the more important one.

steps.title: Make it safe where it is used
steps.text:
Data becomes dangerous when it is placed into a context that gives some characters special meaning: a SQL statement, an HTML page, a shell command, a file path. What counts as dangerous depends on that destination. An apostrophe matters in SQL and not in a file name. A `<` matters in HTML and not in SQL.

So no single cleaning step at the entrance can make a value safe for every later use. The defence belongs at each exit, in the form that suits that destination.

| Destination | Defence |
| --- | --- |
| A SQL statement | Parameters, never pasted text |
| An HTML page | Output encoding for the exact place in the page |
| A shell command | Avoid the shell. Pass arguments as a list |
| A file path | Use a generated name. Check the final path stays inside the allowed folder |
| A URL to fetch | An allowlist of hosts |
| A log line | Remove line breaks, so one entry cannot pose as two |

Validate at the entrance, and encode or parameterise at each exit. Each catches what the other misses. The next two modules cover the two most important exits in detail.

steps.title: The filter
steps.text: A developer protects a comment field by removing the text `<script>` from every comment before saving it.

steps.title: Files and paths
steps.text:
Uploaded files and file names need extra care, since a file system gives special meaning to parts of a name.

**Path traversal.** If the code builds a path from user input, a name such as `../../etc/passwd` climbs out of the intended folder. The `..` means "parent folder". Never build a path from a name the user supplied. Generate your own name, such as a random identifier, and keep the original only as a label in the database.

**File type.** The declared type and the file extension are both chosen by the sender. A file called `photo.jpg` can contain anything. Check the content, limit the size, and store uploads where they can never be executed as code: outside the web root, or in separate object storage, served with a type you set.

**Size and count.** An upload with no size limit is a way to fill your disk. Set limits on the size of a file, of a request and of the number of files.

steps.title: Requests your server makes
steps.text:
Some features fetch a URL the user supplies: "import from a link", a webhook address, a preview of a web page. The server then makes a request to wherever the user says.

The danger is that your server sits inside your network. It can reach internal services, admin panels and cloud metadata addresses that the user cannot reach directly. A user who supplies an internal address gets your server to fetch it for them. This is **server-side request forgery** (SSRF).

Defend with an allowlist of permitted hosts where possible. Otherwise, resolve the name and refuse private, loopback and link-local addresses, do not follow redirects blindly, and run the fetching from a part of the network that can reach nothing internal.

steps.title: Structured data and limits
steps.text:
Parsers are part of the attack surface as well.

- **Limit depth and size.** Deeply nested JSON or a huge array can exhaust memory.
- **Reject unknown fields** where you can, or at least ignore them explicitly.
- **Do not bind request data straight onto internal objects.** If a request to update a profile is copied field by field onto the user record, a sender who adds `"is_admin": true` may become an administrator. This is called **mass assignment**. List the fields each endpoint accepts.
- **Turn off features you do not need** in parsers, such as external entities in XML.

steps.title: The extra field
steps.text: An endpoint updates a user's profile. The code takes the JSON body and copies every field in it onto the user's database record. The form in the page sends `name` and `bio`.

steps.title: Exercise: review the inputs
steps.text:
An endpoint lets a user upload a profile picture and choose how it is shown.

```text
POST /profile/picture
fields:  file        the image
         filename    used as the name to save under
         size        "small", "medium" or "large"
         user_id     whose profile to update
         source_url  optional: fetch the image from this address instead
```

For each of the five inputs, say what could go wrong and how you would handle it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
| Input | Risk | Handling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `file` | Not an image. Very large. Contains something harmful | Limit the size. Check the content is a real image by decoding it. Re-encode it to a fresh image. Store it in object storage, never in a folder that can run code |
| `filename` | Path traversal. Overwriting another file. Odd characters | Ignore it for storage. Generate a random name. Keep the original only as a label, encoded when shown |
| `size` | An unexpected value used later in a path or a query | Allowlist: one of three values. Use your own constant for the matching entry |
| `user_id` | Changing someone else's picture | Do not accept it at all. Take the user from the session |
| `source_url` | The server fetching internal addresses (SSRF) | Best: remove the feature. Otherwise allow only `https`, resolve the host and refuse private addresses, limit size and time, and do not follow redirects to other hosts |

Two of the five are best handled by not accepting the input at all. That is often the strongest validation there is. A value the server already knows should never be taken from the request.

lessons.title: Injection
lessons.intro:
Injection happens when data supplied by a user is treated as part of a command. This module covers how it works in SQL and in shell commands, and the one defence that removes the whole class of bug.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy. The examples show how a flaw arises so that you can recognise and prevent it in your own code.

steps.title: Code and data in one string
steps.text:
Many systems accept commands as text: a database takes SQL, a shell takes a command line, a template engine takes a template. When a program builds such a command by joining fixed text and a user's value into one string, the receiver cannot tell which part came from where. It reads the whole string as a command.

If the user's value contains characters that mean something in that language, the value can end the data part early and add commands of its own. That is **injection**.

Every form of injection has the same cause: code and data mixed in one string. Every reliable fix has the same shape: keep them apart.

steps.title: SQL injection
steps.text:
Suppose a login check builds its query by joining strings. In plain words, the program does this:

```text
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"
```

With the email `ana@example.com`, the database receives a normal query.

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'ana@example.com'
```

Now suppose the value sent as the email is `x' OR '1'='1`. The database receives this:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'x' OR '1'='1'
```

The apostrophe in the input closed the text value. The rest was read as SQL. The condition is now true for every row, so the query returns every user.

The same flaw lets an attacker read other tables, change data or delete it, depending on what the database account is allowed to do. It has been one of the most common serious flaws in web applications for decades.

steps.title: Parameters
steps.text:
The fix is to send the statement and the values separately. The statement contains placeholders, and each value travels beside it as a **parameter**.

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1
```

The database parses the statement first, with the placeholder standing for "one value goes here". Then it receives the value. Whatever the value contains, it is used as one value. An apostrophe in it is an apostrophe in an email address. It cannot become SQL, because the command was fixed before the value arrived.

This is called a **parameterised query** or a prepared statement. Every database library supports it. Use it for every value, every time, including values you believe are safe. There is no need to judge each case, and no way to judge one wrongly.

steps.title: What parameters cannot do
steps.text:
A parameter can stand for a value. It cannot stand for a table name, a column name or a keyword such as `ASC`.

So a feature like "sort by the column the user chose" cannot be parameterised directly. The safe pattern is an allowlist. Compare the user's choice with a fixed list, and put your own text into the statement.

```text
allowed = { "name": "name", "price": "price", "newest": "created_at" }
column  = allowed[user_choice]        refuse if it is not in the list
query   = "SELECT ... ORDER BY " + column
```

The text joined into the query comes from your list. The user only chose which entry.

Query builders and ORMs (libraries that generate SQL from objects) use parameters for you in their normal methods. They also have "raw" methods that accept a string. Injection in modern code is nearly always found there.

steps.title: Parameterised or not
steps.text:
A search endpoint runs this, where `term` comes from the user and is sent as a parameter, and `order` comes from the user and is joined into the string:

```text
"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE $1 ORDER BY " + order
```

steps.title: Command injection
steps.text:
The same flaw exists when a program builds a shell command from user input.

Suppose a service makes thumbnails by running a command line built from a file name:

```text
run_shell("convert " + filename + " thumbnail.png")
```

A shell gives meaning to many characters. A `;` ends one command and starts another. If the file name sent is `photo.jpg; rm -rf /srv/data`, the shell runs two commands, and the second one deletes data.

There are two defences, in order of preference.

1. **Do not use a shell.** Call a library function for the task. Most things a shell command does can be done by a library.
2. **If you must run a program, pass arguments as a list.** Every language has a way to start a program with its arguments as separate items and no shell in between. The program receives each argument exactly as given. No character is special, because nothing is parsing a command line.

steps.title: The same flaw in other places
steps.text:
Wherever a string is interpreted, injection is possible.

- **Templates.** If user input is used as a template, and not as a value given to a template, the template engine may execute expressions inside it.
- **Queries to other stores.** Document databases and search engines have query languages too. Passing a user's JSON straight in as a query lets the user add operators.
- **LDAP, XPath, regular expressions.** Each has characters with special meaning.
- **Log files.** A line break in input lets one request write what looks like a second, false log entry.
- **Email headers.** A line break in a "subject" value can add recipients.
- **Dynamic code.** Functions that evaluate a string as code must never receive user input.

The question to ask of any code is: is a string being built here that something else will interpret? If so, find that system's way of passing values separately.

steps.title: Limit the damage
steps.text:
Parameters prevent the flaw. A second layer limits what happens if a flaw slips through anyway.

- **Least privilege for the database account.** The account the application uses should be able to read and write its own tables and nothing more. It should not be able to drop tables, read other databases or act as an administrator. An injected command can do only what the account may do.
- **Separate accounts** for separate jobs: one for the application, another for migrations, another, read-only, for reporting.
- **Do not show database errors to users.** A raw error message tells an attacker the table names and the kind of database. Log the detail and show a generic message.

steps.title: How it is found
steps.text:
You do not have to wait for an attacker.

- **Code review.** Look for strings built with user input that are passed to a database, a shell or an evaluator. In a review, any string joining near SQL deserves a second look.
- **Static analysis.** Tools that read code can flag these patterns automatically.
- **Tests.** A test that sends an apostrophe in every text field catches the crudest cases.

steps.title: The helpful error
steps.text:
A site's search box shows this when a user types an apostrophe:

```text
ERROR: syntax error at or near "'" in
SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE title LIKE '%'%'
```

steps.title: Exercise: find the injection
steps.text:
A reporting service has these four pieces of code, written here in plain words. For each, say whether it is open to injection, and how to fix it.

1. `"SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = " + id`, where `id` comes from the URL and "is always a number".
2. A parameterised query: `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE customer_id = $1`, with the customer ID from the session.
3. `"SELECT * FROM " + table + " LIMIT 10"`, where `table` comes from a dropdown in the page.
4. `run_shell("pdf-export --out /tmp/" + name + ".pdf")`, where `name` is a report title typed by the user.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Open.** "Always a number" is a belief about the page, and the request can carry anything. Send `id` as a parameter. Also validate that it is an integer and reject it otherwise, which gives a clean error and a second layer.

2. **Safe.** The value is a parameter, and it comes from the server's own session, not from the request. Nothing to change.

3. **Open.** A table name cannot be a parameter, and a dropdown is no restriction, since the request can be sent by hand. Keep a fixed list of the tables that may be shown, look the user's choice up in it, and join your own text. Ask also whether users should be choosing tables at all.

4. **Open, twice.** The title goes into a shell command, so `;` or `$( )` in it runs other commands. It is also used in a file path, so `../` in it writes outside `/tmp`. Start the program with a list of arguments and no shell. Generate the file name yourself, such as a random identifier, and keep the title only as a label.

Item 1 is the most instructive. The developer was not careless. They trusted a fact about their own page. Parameters remove the need for that trust.

lessons.title: Cross-site scripting
lessons.intro:
Cross-site scripting is injection into a web page. A user's text is placed into HTML in a way that lets the browser run it as script. This module covers how it happens, what such a script can do, and the layers that prevent it.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: The flaw
steps.text:
A page is built from fixed HTML and from data. When the data is a user's text and it is placed into the page unchanged, the browser cannot tell it from the page's own markup. Suppose a page shows a search term back to the user by putting it straight into the HTML. If the term is `shoes`, the result is harmless. ```html

Results for: shoes

``` If the "term" is a script tag, the browser receives this and runs it: ```html

Results for:

``` This is **cross-site scripting**, shortened to XSS. It is the same mistake as SQL injection, code and data mixed in one string, with HTML as the language and the victim's browser as the interpreter.

steps.title: What an injected script can do
steps.text:
A script that runs in a page runs as that site, with everything the site's own scripts can do, in the browser of whoever is looking at the page.

- Read anything on the page: messages, account details, tokens held in the page.
- Send requests to the site as the logged-in user: change the email address, make a purchase, post content.
- Change what the page shows: a false login form, altered payment details.
- Record what the user types.
- Read cookies and browser storage, unless they are protected.

The attacker does not need the victim's password. They are using the victim's own logged-in session, from inside it. If the victim is an administrator, the script has an administrator's rights.

steps.title: Three kinds
steps.text:
| Kind | Where the script comes from | Who is hit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stored | Saved in the database (a comment, a profile name) and shown to others | Everyone who views it |
| Reflected | Carried in the request (a link with a crafted parameter) and echoed in the response | Whoever opens the link |
| DOM-based | Never reaches the server. Page script reads it from the URL and writes it into the page | Whoever opens the link |

Stored XSS is the most serious, since it needs no trick to deliver. A script in a comment runs for every visitor to that page, including staff who moderate it.

steps.title: Output encoding
steps.text:
The main defence is **output encoding** (also called escaping). When data is placed into HTML, each character that has meaning in HTML is replaced by a code that the browser displays as that character and does not act on.

| Character | Replaced by |
| --- | --- |
| `<` | `<` |
| `>` | `>` |
| `&` | `&` |
| `"` | `"` |
| `'` | `'` |

After encoding, the script tag from the earlier example arrives as text. The browser shows the characters on the screen and runs nothing.

Encode at the moment of output, not at input. Store the user's text as they typed it. The same text may later go into HTML, a JSON response, a CSV file or an email, and each needs different treatment. Encoding once at the entrance gets all but one of them wrong.

steps.title: Let the template engine do it
steps.text:
Nobody should encode by hand. Modern template engines and front-end frameworks encode every value by default. A value placed in a template is treated as text unless you explicitly say otherwise.

That makes XSS in modern code a matter of the exceptions. Look for these.

- **The "raw" or "unsafe" output feature** of the template engine, which switches encoding off for one value.
- **Setting HTML from a string in script**, such as assigning to `innerHTML`. Assigning to `textContent` is the safe counterpart.
- **Framework escape hatches** with names that warn you, such as `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` or `v-html`.
- **Values placed where HTML encoding is the wrong kind**, covered in the next section.

In a code review, search for those features by name. Each use needs a reason, and proof that the value cannot contain user input.

steps.title: Context matters
steps.text:
HTML encoding is right for text between tags. A value placed somewhere else in the page needs the encoding of that place, or should not be put there at all. | Where the value goes | What is needed | | --- | --- | | Between tags: `

VALUE

` | HTML encoding | | In a quoted attribute: `title="VALUE"` | Attribute encoding, and the quotes must be there | | In a link target: `href="VALUE"` | Check that the scheme is `http` or `https`. A `javascript:` URL runs script when clicked | | Inside a script block | Avoid it. Put the data in a data attribute or a JSON block, and read it from script | | Inside a style block or attribute | Avoid it | The link case is the one most often missed. HTML encoding leaves `javascript:alert(1)` unchanged, since it contains no special HTML characters. A "website" field in a profile that is used as a link target needs its scheme checked.

steps.title: The link field
steps.text: A profile page shows a user's website as a link. The template engine HTML-encodes the value automatically. A user sets their website to `javascript:` followed by some script.

steps.title: When users may write HTML
steps.text:
Some features need users to supply formatted content: a rich-text editor, a comment with bold and links. Encoding everything would show the tags as text.

The answer is **sanitisation**: parse the HTML and keep only an allowlist of harmless tags and attributes, such as `b`, `i`, `p`, `a` with a checked `href`. Everything else is dropped.

Use a well-maintained sanitising library for this. Writing your own with pattern matching does not work, since HTML has too many odd corners. A safer design where it fits is to store a simple format such as Markdown and generate the HTML yourself.

steps.title: Content Security Policy
steps.text:
A **Content Security Policy** (CSP) is a response header that tells the browser which scripts the page is allowed to run. It is a second layer: if an injection gets past the encoding, the browser may still refuse to run it.


This policy says that scripts may be loaded only from the site's own origin. A script tag written into the page by an attacker is inline script, which the policy does not allow, so the browser does not run it.

A strict policy requires that the page has no inline script of its own, which older sites often do. Policies can be tried in a report-only mode first, where violations are reported and nothing is blocked.

CSP reduces the damage from a mistake. It does not replace encoding.

steps.title: Protect the session cookie
steps.text:
One more layer limits what a successful script can take. A cookie marked `HttpOnly` cannot be read by script at all. The browser still sends it with requests, and script in the page cannot see its value.

A session cookie should always be `HttpOnly`. An injected script can then still act as the user while the page is open, and it cannot copy the session to use later from elsewhere.

This is also the reason not to keep session tokens in browser storage that scripts can read. Anything a script can read, an injected script can read.

steps.title: The moderator
steps.text: A forum encodes comments correctly on the public pages. The internal moderation tool, written later by another team, displays reported comments using the template engine's "raw" output, so that moderators "see the comment exactly as posted".

steps.title: Exercise: review the page
steps.text:
A product review page does the following. For each item, say whether it is safe, and what to change.

1. Shows the reviewer's display name between tags, through the template engine's normal output.
2. Shows the review text using the engine's "raw" output, because reviews may contain line breaks.
3. Puts the reviewer's name into a script block: `var author = "NAME";`
4. Shows a link to the reviewer's own website, with the address taken from their profile.
5. Reads a `highlight` parameter from the URL in page script and writes it into the page with `innerHTML`.
6. Sets the session cookie without the `HttpOnly` flag, because a script needs to read it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Safe.** Normal template output encodes the value. 2. **Unsafe: stored XSS.** Raw output of user text runs any script in a review, for every visitor. Use normal encoded output, and keep the line breaks with a style rule that preserves them, or by converting line breaks to `
` after encoding. 3. **Unsafe.** HTML encoding does not protect inside a script block. A name containing a quote, or ``, breaks out. Put the name in a data attribute, which is an ordinary encoded attribute, and read it from script. 4. **Unsafe unless the scheme is checked.** A `javascript:` address would run on click. Accept only `http` and `https` when the profile is saved, and check again when the link is rendered. 5. **Unsafe: DOM-based XSS.** Text from the URL is written as HTML. Use `textContent`, which treats it as text. 6. **A weak layer.** With no `HttpOnly`, any of the flaws above lets a script copy the session. Mark the cookie `HttpOnly`, and change the script so that it does not need the cookie's value. A Content Security Policy that forbids inline script would have blunted items 2, 3 and 5. It is worth adding, and each of those still needs its own fix.

lessons.title: Authentication
lessons.intro:
Authentication is how a system decides who is making a request. Every other control depends on it. This module covers the ways to prove identity, how login is attacked, and how to build the flows around it.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: Authentication and authorization
steps.text:
Two words sound alike and mean different things.

- **Authentication** answers "who are you?" It establishes an identity.
- **Authorization** answers "what are you allowed to do?" It checks that identity against a rule.

A system needs both, and they fail in different ways. Weak authentication lets an attacker become someone else. Weak authorization lets a properly logged-in user reach things that are not theirs. This module is about the first. A later one covers the second.

steps.title: Factors
steps.text:
Identity is proven with one or more **factors**, of three kinds.

| Factor | What it is | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Something you know | A secret in your head | Password, PIN |
| Something you have | An object in your possession | Phone with an authenticator app, security key |
| Something you are | A feature of your body | Fingerprint, face |

**Multi-factor authentication** (MFA) asks for two of different kinds. Its strength comes from the difference. Someone who has stolen a password from a breach on another site does not also have the victim's phone.

Two passwords are not two factors. A password and a "secret question" are both things you know.

steps.title: How passwords fail
steps.text:
Passwords are the most common factor and the weakest. The attacks on them rarely involve guessing at random.

- **Credential stuffing.** People reuse passwords. When one site is breached, the leaked email and password pairs are tried on every other site automatically. This is the largest source of account takeover.
- **Password spraying.** One common password, such as `Winter2025!`, is tried against many accounts. It stays under per-account lockout limits.
- **Phishing.** The user is tricked into typing the password into a false copy of the site.
- **Brute force.** Many passwords are tried against one account. It works only when nothing limits the attempts.

Three of these four succeed however complex the password is. A long, unique password that has been phished is as lost as a short one.

steps.title: A sensible password policy
steps.text:
Older advice asked for symbols, digits and a change every 90 days. It produced passwords like `Password1!` followed by `Password2!`. Current guidance, such as that from NIST, is simpler and works better.

- **Length matters most.** Require a reasonable minimum, such as 12 characters, and allow long passphrases. Do not set a low maximum.
- **Check against known breached and common passwords**, and refuse those.
- **Do not force regular changes.** Require a change when there is evidence of compromise.
- **Do not impose composition rules** such as "one symbol and one digit".
- **Allow pasting**, so that password managers work. A manager gives each site a long random password, which defeats credential stuffing.

steps.title: Limit the attempts
steps.text:
A login endpoint with no limit can be tried millions of times.

- **Rate limit** by account and by client address. A handful of failures should slow further attempts sharply.
- **Delay, do not lock for ever.** A hard lockout after five failures lets anyone lock a victim out by guessing wrong on purpose. Growing delays, or a temporary lock, avoid that.
- **Watch for the pattern across accounts.** Spraying and stuffing show up as many accounts failing from few sources, not as one account failing many times.
- **Tell the user.** A notice of a new login from an unfamiliar device lets the real owner react.

steps.title: Multi-factor authentication
steps.text:
MFA is the most effective single defence against account takeover. A stolen or reused password is no longer enough. The kinds differ a great deal in strength.

| Method | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code sent by SMS | Better than nothing | Phone numbers can be taken over. Codes can be phished |
| Code from an authenticator app (TOTP) | Good | The code can still be phished and replayed within seconds |
| Push approval on a phone | Good | Users approve prompts they did not start, when sent many |
| Security key or passkey (WebAuthn) | Strongest | Needs device support and a recovery plan |

A security key or **passkey** is different in kind from the others. The device holds a private key and signs a challenge, and the signature is bound to the real site's address. A false site at another address gets a signature that is useless on the real one. That is why this method resists phishing and the code-based ones do not.

Offer the strongest method you can, and require MFA for administrators and for any account that can do serious harm.

steps.title: Which protects
steps.text: A user's password for a shop is the same one they used on a forum that was breached last year. The shop requires a code from an authenticator app at login.

steps.title: Do not reveal who has an account
steps.text:
A login form that says "no account with that email" for one input and "wrong password" for another tells anyone which emails are registered. That is **user enumeration**. It gives an attacker a list of real accounts to target, and on some sites the mere fact of having an account is private.

Give the same answer in both cases: "email or password is incorrect". Apply the same care to every place that could leak the fact:

- the registration form ("this email is already in use"),
- the password reset form,
- the time taken to respond, which can differ when the account exists.

For registration and reset, the usual answer is to always say "if that address has an account, we have sent an email", and to put the real information in the email.

steps.title: Password reset is a second login
steps.text:
A reset flow lets someone into an account without the password. It is therefore exactly as sensitive as login, and it is attacked more often, since it is usually built with less care.

A sound reset flow:

1. The user asks for a reset. The response is the same whether or not the account exists.
2. The server creates a **token**: long, random and unguessable. It stores a hash of it, with an expiry time of an hour or less.
3. The token is sent in a link to the address on file.
4. Opening the link allows one password change. The token is then deleted, and so are all other reset tokens for the account.
5. All existing sessions for the account are ended, and the user is told by email that the password changed.

Faults to avoid: tokens that can be guessed or that never expire, tokens that work more than once, security questions (the answers are often public), and emailing the old or a new password in plain text.

steps.title: Do not build what you can borrow
steps.text:
Authentication has many details, and a mistake in any one opens accounts. Where you can, use something built and tested by specialists.

- **A well-used library or framework feature** for login, sessions and password storage.
- **Single sign-on** (SSO) through an identity provider, using a standard such as OpenID Connect. Your application never sees a password. It receives a signed statement of who the user is. One strong login, with MFA, then covers many applications, and removing a person's access happens in one place.

When you use these, the remaining work is to use them correctly: validate what the provider sends, and keep the library updated.

steps.title: Re-authenticate for sensitive actions
steps.text:
A logged-in session can be left open on a shared computer or taken over. For actions with serious consequences, ask the user to prove their identity again at that moment: changing the email or password, adding a payment method, exporting all data, deleting the account.

Changing the email address deserves particular care. It is the reset channel. Whoever controls it controls the account. Ask for the password, notify the old address, and consider a delay before the change takes effect.

steps.title: The reset link
steps.text: A site's password reset link looks like `https://app.example.com/reset?user=5521&t=1741096931`, where `t` is the time the reset was requested, in seconds. The link never expires.

steps.title: Exercise: review the login
steps.text:
A web application's account system works like this.

1. Passwords must be 8 characters with a digit and a symbol, and must be changed every 60 days.
2. Login shows "unknown email" or "wrong password".
3. After 5 failures an account is locked until an administrator unlocks it.
4. MFA by SMS is optional and switched off by default, including for administrators.
5. Password reset asks "What was your first pet's name?" and, on a correct answer, shows a new password on the screen.
6. Changing the account's email address needs no confirmation.

List the problem with each and what you would do. Then say which change gives the largest improvement.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Outdated rules.** Short passwords with forced changes produce predictable patterns. Require 12 or more characters, refuse known breached passwords, drop composition rules and forced changes, and allow pasting.
2. **User enumeration.** Use one message for both cases, and the same on registration and reset.
3. **Lockout as a weapon.** Anyone can lock any account, administrators included, with five bad guesses. Use growing delays and rate limits by address, and unlock automatically after a time.
4. **Weak and optional MFA.** Require MFA for administrators. Offer an authenticator app and passkeys, with SMS only as a fallback.
5. **A reset anyone can pass.** A pet's name is often public or guessable, and the new password appears on screen to whoever answered. Replace it with a random, short-lived, single-use link sent to the address on file. End existing sessions afterwards and notify the owner.
6. **Silent takeover.** An attacker in a session changes the email and then owns the reset channel. Require the password again, notify the old address, and confirm the new one before switching.

**The largest improvement** is requiring MFA, starting with administrators. It defeats credential stuffing and spraying, which are the most common attacks, even while the other faults are still being fixed. The reset flow comes second, since today it is a way around the password entirely.

lessons.title: Store passwords safely
lessons.intro:
Sooner or later a database is copied by someone who should not have it. How passwords were stored decides whether that is an incident or a catastrophe. This module covers why passwords are hashed, why an ordinary hash is not enough, and what to use.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: Plan for the database being stolen
steps.text:
Design password storage on the assumption that an attacker will one day hold a full copy of the users table. It happens through SQL injection, a leaked backup, a misconfigured storage bucket or an insider.

The goal is that the copy does not give them the passwords. That matters beyond your own site. People reuse passwords, so a leaked password opens that person's email, bank and workplace accounts too.

So the first rule is absolute: never store a password in a form from which it can be read back. Not in plain text, and not encrypted either.

steps.title: Why not encrypt them
steps.text:
Encryption is reversible by design. Whoever has the key can turn the stored value back into the password. The application needs the key to do its work, so the key sits on the same systems as the data. An attacker who can copy the database can usually reach the key as well.

There is also no reason for the system to be able to read a password. To check a login, it only needs to know whether what was typed matches what was set. That can be done without ever being able to recover the original.

A site that can email you your existing password is storing it reversibly. That is a sign of a serious flaw.

steps.title: Hashing
steps.text:
A **hash function** turns any input into a fixed-size value, the **hash**, with two properties that matter here.

- **One way.** Given the hash, there is no practical method to compute the input.
- **Deterministic.** The same input always gives the same hash.

To store a password, store its hash. To check a login, hash what was typed and compare the two hashes. The system can verify a password without being able to tell anyone what it is.

steps.title: Why a fast hash fails
steps.text:
General-purpose hash functions such as SHA-256 are built to be fast. A modern graphics card computes billions of them per second. Speed is right for checking files and wrong for passwords.

An attacker with the stolen hashes does not reverse them. They guess. Take a candidate password, hash it, and compare the result with every stolen hash. At billions of guesses a second, every common password, every dictionary word with a digit on the end and every password from earlier breaches is tried within minutes.

Two further weaknesses make it worse when plain hashes are used.

- **Identical passwords have identical hashes.** Crack one, and every user with that password is cracked. The most common hash in the table is the most common password.
- **Precomputed tables.** Lists of hashes for billions of likely passwords already exist. Looking a hash up takes no computation at all.

steps.title: Salt
steps.text:
A **salt** is a random value, different for every user, that is combined with the password before hashing. It is stored beside the hash, in the open.

A salt does two things.

- Two users with the same password get different hashes, since their salts differ.
- Precomputed tables become useless. A table would have to be built separately for every salt.

A salt does not need to be secret. Its job is to be unique, so that an attacker must attack each password separately and cannot attack them all at once.

steps.title: Slow on purpose
steps.text:
A salt forces the attacker to work on each password separately. It does not make each guess slower. The remaining defence is to use a hash function that is slow and costly by design. These are called **password hashing functions**.

| Function | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Argon2id | The current first choice. Costs both time and memory |
| scrypt | Also memory-hard. A sound choice |
| bcrypt | Older and still acceptable. Input is limited to 72 bytes |
| PBKDF2 | Acceptable with a high iteration count. Used where standards require it |

Each takes a **cost setting** (also called a work factor). Tune it so that one hash takes a noticeable fraction of a second on your servers, for example 100 to 300 ms. A real user does not notice that at login. An attacker's rate of guessing falls from billions per second to a few thousand or less.

The functions that also need a lot of memory, Argon2id and scrypt, resist graphics cards and custom hardware best, since memory is hard to multiply cheaply.

These functions generate and store the salt for you. Their output is one string that contains the algorithm, the cost settings, the salt and the hash. Use a maintained library, and do not assemble the pieces yourself.

steps.title: Which table
steps.text: A breach exposes a users table. Passwords were stored as unsalted SHA-256 hashes. Of 2 million users, 31,000 share the same hash value.

steps.title: Raising the cost over time
steps.text:
Hardware gets faster, so a cost setting that was right five years ago is too low today. The stored string records the settings each hash was made with, which allows a gradual upgrade.

At each successful login, the system has the password in hand for a moment. If the stored hash uses old settings or an old algorithm, compute a new hash with the current settings and replace it. Active users are upgraded without noticing.

Accounts that never log in keep their old hashes. For a migration away from something weak, such as unsalted hashes, either wrap the old hash inside the new function at once, or expire those passwords and require a reset.

steps.title: Pepper
steps.text:
A **pepper** is a secret value added to every password before hashing, kept outside the database, in a secrets store or a hardware module. An attacker who has only the database then cannot test guesses at all, since they lack the pepper.

It is an extra layer, useful where the database is the more likely thing to leak. It adds work: the pepper must be protected and cannot be changed easily. It is optional. A slow, salted hash is not.

steps.title: Handling the password in transit
steps.text:
A password also has to travel from the user to the hash function.

- **Always over TLS.** A password sent over plain HTTP can be read on the way.
- **Never in a URL.** URLs are stored in browser history, server logs and proxy logs. Send credentials in the request body.
- **Never in logs.** A common accident is logging whole request bodies for debugging, which fills the logs with passwords. Exclude credential fields from logging explicitly.
- **Do not limit the length to something small**, or forbid characters. The hash output has a fixed size whatever the input. Do set a generous upper bound, such as a few hundred characters, so that nobody can make the server hash megabytes.

steps.title: Compare carefully
steps.text:
When the system compares secrets, such as tokens or hashes, it should use a comparison that takes the same time whether the values differ at the first character or the last. An ordinary comparison stops at the first difference, and the time it takes can leak how much of a guess was right. This is a **timing attack**.

Password hashing libraries do this correctly in their verify function. Use that function, and do not compare hash strings yourself.

steps.title: Other secrets are not passwords
steps.text:
The slow hash is for secrets chosen by people, which are short and guessable. A long random token, such as an API key or a reset token with 128 bits or more of randomness, cannot be guessed in the first place.

Such tokens should still be stored hashed, so that a database copy does not hand them over. For these a fast hash such as SHA-256 is acceptable, since nobody can run through the possibilities. The slow function would only add delay to every API request.

steps.title: The login that logged
steps.text: To debug a login problem, a developer adds a line that writes the full request body of every failed login to the application log. The log is kept for a year and can be read by 40 engineers and a log vendor.

steps.title: Exercise: review the storage
steps.text:
A ten-year-old application stores passwords like this.

- The users table has a `password_md5` column, holding the MD5 hash of the password. MD5 is a fast hash that is no longer considered safe for any security use.
- There is no salt.
- Passwords are limited to 16 characters, and the characters `'`, `"` and `;` are forbidden.
- A "forgot password" feature emails a new password in plain text, which the user keeps until they change it.
- There are 3 million accounts. About 40% have not logged in for two years.

Say what is wrong with each point. Then describe a migration to a sound scheme that does not require every user to reset their password on the same day.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Problems**

- **A fast, broken hash.** MD5 is computed at tens of billions per second, and tables of MD5 hashes for common passwords are published. A stolen table is effectively plain text for most users.
- **No salt.** Equal passwords share a hash, and precomputed tables apply directly.
- **Length and character limits.** A 16-character cap blocks passphrases. The forbidden characters suggest that passwords are being joined into SQL somewhere, which is a second problem to look for.
- **A password by email.** It sits in an inbox indefinitely, and it shows the system chooses passwords for users. Use a single-use reset link.

**Migration**

1. **Wrap at once.** For every row, compute `argon2id(old_md5_hash)` with a fresh salt and store that, marked as "wrapped". Delete the MD5 column. From this moment a stolen database no longer contains fast hashes, for all 3 million accounts, including the inactive ones. No user is involved.
2. **Upgrade at login.** When a user logs in, compute MD5 of what they typed, verify it against the wrapped value, and on success store a plain `argon2id(password)` and mark the row as current.
3. **Lift the limits** on length and characters at the same time, and fix whatever code made them necessary.
4. **Replace the reset flow** with a random, expiring, single-use link.
5. **After some months**, expire the passwords of accounts still marked "wrapped" and require a reset at their next visit, or remove accounts that are long abandoned.

Step 1 is the one that matters most. It removes the danger on the first day, without waiting for anyone to log in.

questions.prompt: What does an attacker learn at once?

choices.text: Nothing, since SHA-256 cannot be reversed
choices.feedback: It does not need reversing. The repetition itself is information.

choices.text: That 31,000 users chose the same password, almost certainly a very common one, which will be found in seconds
choices.feedback: Without a salt, equal passwords give equal hashes. The most frequent hash is the weakest password, and cracking it once opens all 31,000 accounts.

choices.text: The passwords of all 2 million users
choices.feedback: Not at once. Common ones fall quickly, and long random ones may never be found.

questions.prompt: What has been created?

choices.text: A useful debugging aid with no security effect
choices.feedback: The request body of a login contains the password.

choices.text: A plain-text store of passwords, including near-misses of real ones, readable by many people
choices.feedback: Failed logins are often the right password with one typing error, or the user's password for another site. The careful hashing in the database is bypassed by the log beside it.

choices.text: A risk only if the log is leaked outside the company
choices.feedback: Forty readers and a vendor is already wide exposure. Passwords should be readable by nobody.

lessons.title: Sessions and tokens
lessons.intro:
HTTP does not remember who you are from one request to the next. After login, something has to carry that fact. This module covers the two ways to do it, how each is stolen or misused, and how to end a session properly.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: The problem
steps.text:
A user proves their identity once, at login. Every later request must show that it comes from that same user, without asking for the password again.

The answer is always a **credential** issued at login and presented with each request. Anyone who holds it is treated as the user. So this credential is as valuable as the password for as long as it is valid, and it needs the same protection.

There are two designs: a session ID that points at data on the server, and a token that carries the data itself.

steps.title: Server-side sessions
steps.text:
At login, the server creates a **session**: a record that says "this session belongs to user 17, started at this time". It stores the record in a database or a cache, and gives the browser a **session ID**, which is a long random string.

The browser sends the ID with every request, in a cookie. The server looks the ID up and finds the user.

The ID carries no information. It is only a key to the record. That gives this design its main strength: the server is in control. To log a user out, or to cut off a stolen session, delete the record. The next request with that ID finds nothing.

steps.title: The session ID must be unguessable
steps.text:
If an attacker can guess or predict a valid ID, they are logged in as its owner. So an ID must be:

- **Long and random**, from a cryptographically secure random source, with at least 128 bits of randomness.
- **Never derived** from the user ID, the time or a counter.
- **Replaced at login.** If the ID from before login is kept afterwards, an attacker who planted a known ID in the victim's browser shares the session once the victim logs in. This is **session fixation**. Issue a fresh ID whenever the level of privilege changes.

Use the session mechanism of your framework. It does these things already.

steps.title: Cookie attributes
steps.text:
A session cookie should be set with attributes that limit where it goes and who can read it.

| Attribute | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `HttpOnly` | Script in the page cannot read the cookie. An injected script cannot copy the session |
| `Secure` | The cookie is sent only over HTTPS, never in the clear |
| `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` | The cookie is not sent on most requests started by other sites. The next module explains why |
| `Path` and `Domain` | Limit which URLs receive it. Keep the domain as narrow as possible |
| An expiry | Without one, the cookie lasts until the browser closes. With one, it persists |


All three of `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite` belong on every session cookie. Leaving one out removes a layer for no benefit.

steps.title: Tokens that carry their own data
steps.text:
The second design puts the information in the credential. The best-known format is the **JSON Web Token** (JWT). It has three parts joined by dots.

- A **header** that says how it is signed.
- A **payload** of **claims**: who the user is, when the token expires, who issued it.
- A **signature** over the first two, made with a key that only the issuer holds.

A server that receives the token checks the signature and the expiry and then trusts the claims, without looking anything up. That makes tokens convenient when many separate services need to verify a user, since none of them needs access to a shared session store.

Two facts about a JWT are often misunderstood.

- The payload is **encoded, not encrypted**. Anyone who holds the token can read it. Never put a secret in it.
- It cannot be changed without breaking the signature. A user who edits `"role": "user"` to `"role": "admin"` produces a token that fails verification, provided the server really verifies.

steps.title: Validate a token completely
steps.text:
A token is only as safe as its verification. Every one of these checks is required.

- **The signature**, using a key you already trust. Fix the algorithm in your own configuration. A classic flaw was to accept whatever algorithm the token's header named, including `none`.
- **The expiry** (`exp`). Reject an expired token.
- **The issuer** (`iss`). It must be the one you expect.
- **The audience** (`aud`). It must be your service. Without this check, a token issued for one service can be replayed against another.

Use a maintained library and configure all four. Hand-written JWT handling is a common source of serious flaws.

steps.title: The trouble with revoking tokens
steps.text:
A self-contained token is valid until it expires. The server looks nothing up, so there is nothing to delete. If a token is stolen, or the user logs out, or an administrator removes someone's access, the token keeps working.

The standard arrangement keeps the damage small.

- A short-lived **access token**, valid for minutes, is sent with each request.
- A long-lived **refresh token** is kept more carefully and used only to obtain new access tokens. It is checked against the server's records each time, so it can be revoked.

When access is removed, the refresh token is revoked. The access token dies by itself within minutes. For cases that cannot wait even that long, services check a list of revoked tokens, which brings back the lookup that tokens were meant to avoid.

| | Server-side session | Self-contained token |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server keeps state | Yes | No |
| Revoke at once | Yes, delete the record | Not without extra machinery |
| Works across many services | Needs a shared store | Yes |
| Readable by the holder | No, the ID means nothing | Yes |
| Good default for | A web application | APIs called by several services |

For an ordinary web application with one backend, a server-side session in a cookie is simpler and safer. Reach for tokens when you have a reason.

steps.title: After the firing
steps.text: A company's internal tool uses JWTs that are valid for 30 days, with no refresh tokens and no revocation list. An employee is dismissed at 10:00, and their account is disabled in the user directory.

steps.title: Where the browser keeps it
steps.text:
In a browser, a credential can live in a cookie or in storage that scripts can read, such as `localStorage`.

Anything script can read, an injected script can steal. One cross-site scripting flaw then hands the attacker a credential they can use from their own machine, for as long as it is valid.

A cookie marked `HttpOnly` cannot be read by script. An injected script can still send requests while the page is open, and it cannot carry the credential away. That is a real difference, and it is why an `HttpOnly` cookie is the better place for a session credential in a web application.

Cookies are sent automatically, which creates the cross-site request problem covered in the next module. `SameSite` is the answer to that.

steps.title: Expiry and logout
steps.text:
A session should not last for ever.

- **Idle timeout.** End the session after a period with no activity. Choose the period by sensitivity: minutes for banking, days for a low-risk site.
- **Absolute timeout.** End it after a maximum age whatever the activity, so a stolen session cannot be kept alive indefinitely.
- **Logout that works.** Delete the session record on the server. Clearing the cookie in the browser alone leaves a credential that still works if someone copied it.
- **End sessions on a password change**, and let users see their active sessions and end them.

steps.title: Which storage
steps.text: A single-page application keeps its access token in `localStorage` and adds it to each request from script. A cross-site scripting flaw is found in its comments page.

steps.title: Exercise: review the session handling
steps.text:
A web application handles sessions as follows.

1. The session ID is the user's numeric ID followed by the login time, for example `5521-1741096931`.
2. The cookie is set with `Set-Cookie: sid=...; Path=/` and nothing else.
3. The ID a visitor has before login is kept after login.
4. Sessions never expire.
5. "Log out" deletes the cookie in the browser.
6. A second service receives a JWT from the first, decodes the payload to get the user ID, and does not check the signature, "because the network is internal".

List the problem with each and the fix.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **A guessable ID.** A user ID and a timestamp can be worked out for any account. Generate IDs from a secure random source with at least 128 bits.
2. **No protective attributes.** The cookie can be read by script, sent over plain HTTP and sent on cross-site requests. Add `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite=Lax`.
3. **Session fixation.** An attacker who sets a known ID in the victim's browser before login is logged in with them afterwards. Issue a new ID at login.
4. **No expiry.** A session stolen once works for ever. Add an idle timeout and an absolute one.
5. **Logout in name only.** The record still exists on the server, so a copied ID keeps working. Delete the server-side session.
6. **An unverified token.** Anyone who can reach the second service can write a payload with any user ID. Verify the signature with a fixed algorithm and a trusted key, and check expiry, issuer and audience. "Internal" is not a control. One compromised machine inside the network can send requests like any other.

Items 1 and 6 let an attacker become any user without stealing anything. They come first.

questions.prompt: Can they still use the tool at 11:00?

choices.text: No, since the account is disabled
choices.feedback: The tool does not consult the directory on each request. It only verifies the token's signature and expiry.

choices.text: Yes, for up to 30 days, with the token they already hold
choices.feedback: A self-contained token stays valid until it expires. Short-lived access tokens with a revocable refresh token would limit this to minutes.

choices.text: Yes, but only to read data
choices.feedback: The token grants whatever it granted before. Nothing about it has changed.

choices.text: Only act while the victim has the page open
choices.feedback: That would be the limit if the credential were in an `HttpOnly` cookie.

choices.text: Read the token and send it to the attacker, who can then use it from anywhere until it expires
choices.feedback: Script-readable storage is readable by injected script. The session leaves the victim's browser entirely.

choices.text: Nothing, since tokens are signed
choices.feedback: The signature stops the token being altered. It does nothing to stop a valid token being copied and used.
