lessons.title: Cross-site requests
lessons.intro:
A browser will send a request to your site from a page on someone else's, and it will attach your cookies when it does. This module covers the attack that follows from that, the rule that keeps sites from reading each other's data, and what CORS does and does not do.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: The same-origin policy
steps.text:
An **origin** is a scheme, a host and a port taken together: `https://app.example.com` is one origin, and `https://api.example.com` is another, since the hosts differ.

Browsers enforce the **same-origin policy**: script running on one origin cannot read responses from another origin. A page on a stranger's site cannot fetch your bank's account page and read the balance, although you are logged in to the bank in another tab.

This rule is the base of web security. Without it, any site you visited could read your email.

Note what the rule covers. It stops a page from **reading** another origin's response. It does not stop a page from **sending** a request to another origin. That gap is what this module is about.

steps.title: Cross-site request forgery
steps.text:
Cookies are attached to requests by the browser automatically, according to where the request is going. Historically it did not matter which page started the request.

So consider a user who is logged in to their bank. In another tab, they open a page controlled by an attacker. That page contains a hidden form addressed to the bank, and submits it with script.

```html
<form action="https://bank.example.com/transfer" method="POST">
  <input type="hidden" name="to" value="attacker-account">
  <input type="hidden" name="amount" value="5000">
</form>
```

The browser sends the request to the bank and attaches the bank's session cookie. The bank sees a correctly authenticated request for a transfer and carries it out. The user saw nothing.

This is **cross-site request forgery** (CSRF). The attacker never sees the cookie and cannot read the response. They do not need to. They only need the action to happen.

steps.title: What makes a request forgeable
steps.text:
A request can be forged when three things are true.

- It **changes something**: transfers money, changes an email address, deletes data.
- It is **authenticated by something the browser attaches automatically**: a cookie, or HTTP basic authentication.
- It **contains nothing the attacker cannot predict**. Every parameter can be filled in by the attacker's page.

Remove any one of the three and the attack fails. The defences below each remove one.

An API that is authenticated only by a token in an `Authorization` header, added by script, is not open to CSRF. The browser does not add that header by itself, so another site's page cannot cause it to be sent.

steps.title: SameSite cookies
steps.text:
The `SameSite` cookie attribute tells the browser when to attach a cookie to a request that another site started.

| Value | The cookie is sent on cross-site requests |
| --- | --- |
| `Strict` | Never. Even following a link from another site arrives logged out |
| `Lax` | Only for top-level navigation with a safe method, such as clicking a link. Not for form posts, images or script requests |
| `None` | Always. Requires `Secure` |

With `SameSite=Lax`, the hidden form post in the example arrives without the session cookie, and the bank treats it as a request from someone not logged in.

Modern browsers apply `Lax` when no value is given. Set it explicitly anyway. Do not depend on a default that has differed between browsers and over time.

`Lax` is the usual choice. `Strict` suits very sensitive applications, at the cost that a link from an email opens a logged-out page.

steps.title: Anti-CSRF tokens
steps.text:
The older, stronger defence removes the predictability. The server gives each session a random **CSRF token** and includes it in every form it renders, as a hidden field. When a form is submitted, the server checks that the token in the request matches the one for the session.

An attacker's page cannot read the token, because the same-origin policy stops it reading your pages. So it cannot build a request the server will accept.

Web frameworks provide this. Turn it on, and do not switch it off for particular endpoints because it was inconvenient.

Use both layers: `SameSite` cookies, and tokens on every state-changing request. Each covers gaps in the other, such as older browsers, or sibling subdomains that count as the same site.

steps.title: Safe methods must be safe
steps.text:
`SameSite=Lax` still sends cookies on a cross-site `GET` navigation. Tokens are normally checked only on `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE`. Both rest on one assumption: a `GET` request never changes anything.

An endpoint such as `GET /account/delete?confirm=yes` breaks that assumption. A plain link or an image tag on another site triggers it, with the cookie attached.

So `GET` must only read. Anything that changes state uses another method. This is an HTTP rule first and a security rule second.

steps.title: The delete link
steps.text: A site's session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`. To remove an item, its pages link to `GET /cart/remove?item=42`. An attacker's page contains a link to that URL, labelled "Claim your prize".

steps.title: CORS
steps.text:
Sometimes you want another origin to read your responses. A front end on `app.example.com` calls an API on `api.example.com`. The same-origin policy blocks that by default.

**CORS** (cross-origin resource sharing) is how a server tells the browser to relax the rule for named origins. The server adds response headers, and the browser decides whether the calling page may see the response.


For requests that are not simple, such as a `PUT` or one with a JSON content type, the browser first sends a **preflight**: an `OPTIONS` request that asks whether the real request is permitted. If the answer does not allow it, the real request is never sent.

steps.title: What CORS is not
steps.text:
CORS is widely misread, and the misreadings cause real flaws.

- **CORS is not a defence.** It loosens a protection. A server with no CORS headers is at its most restrictive.
- **CORS does not stop requests from being sent.** A simple cross-site `POST` reaches your server whatever your CORS settings say. CORS only decides whether the page may read the reply. It does not prevent CSRF.
- **CORS is enforced by browsers only.** A script, a command-line tool or another server ignores it. It is no substitute for authentication.

The dangerous configuration is to echo back whatever origin the request names while also allowing credentials. That tells every site on the internet that it may make authenticated requests to your API and read the answers. It disables the same-origin policy for your users.

List the allowed origins explicitly. A wildcard (`*`) is acceptable only for truly public data, and browsers refuse to combine it with credentials.

steps.title: Clickjacking
steps.text:
A related trick does not forge a request. It gets the user to make a real one. The attacker loads your page in an invisible frame on top of their own page, and places something tempting under the spot where your "Delete account" button sits. The user believes they are clicking the attacker's page.

This is **clickjacking**. The defence is to tell browsers that your pages may not be framed by other sites.


The first header is the current standard. The second is its older form, still worth sending.

steps.title: The permissive API
steps.text: An API sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to whatever value arrives in the request's `Origin` header, and sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. It authenticates with a session cookie that is `SameSite=None`.

steps.title: Exercise: review the endpoints
steps.text:
An application has a browser front end on `https://app.example.com` and an API on `https://api.example.com`. Sessions use a cookie. Review this setup.

1. The session cookie is `Secure; HttpOnly` with no `SameSite` attribute.
2. `POST /api/email` changes the user's email address. It takes `new_email` and has no CSRF token.
3. `GET /api/logout` ends the session.
4. The API answers every request with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.
5. The settings page can be loaded in a frame by any site.
6. A separate public endpoint, `GET /api/status`, returns the service's version and needs no login.

For each, say whether there is a problem and what to do.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Relies on a browser default.** Most browsers now treat a missing value as `Lax`, and that has not always been so. Set `SameSite=Lax` explicitly.
2. **Forgeable, and serious.** It changes state, is authenticated by a cookie, and has one predictable parameter. An attacker's page changes the victim's email to their own and then uses "forgot password" to take the account. Add a CSRF token, set `SameSite`, and require the password to change an email address.
3. **A state change on `GET`.** Any page can log users out with an image tag. It is a nuisance more than a breach, and it shows a habit that will cause worse. Make it a `POST`.
4. **Too broad, though not catastrophic as written.** Browsers refuse to send credentials with a wildcard, so authenticated data stays unreadable to other sites. The risk is the next change, when someone "fixes" a credentials error by echoing the origin. Replace the wildcard with the one real origin, `https://app.example.com`.
5. **Clickjacking.** Send `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'`.
6. **Fine as a public endpoint**, with one remark. The exact version number helps an attacker look up known flaws for it. Consider leaving it out.

Item 2 is the one to fix today. It turns a visit to any hostile page into the loss of the account.

lessons.title: Authorization
lessons.intro:
Authorization decides what a known user may do. Missing or wrong checks here are the most common serious flaw in web applications. This module covers how those checks go missing, how to structure them, and how to give out no more access than is needed.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: The check that is not there
steps.text:
After login, the system knows who is asking. Authorization is the separate question of whether this user may perform this action on this particular thing.

The usual failure is not a wrong rule. It is a missing one. An endpoint checks that the user is logged in and then does what the request says, for whichever record the request names.

In lists of the most serious web application risks, such as the OWASP Top 10, **broken access control** sits at the top. It is easy to introduce, since forgetting a check produces no error and no failing test. Everything works for honest users.

steps.title: Changing the ID
steps.text:
Suppose an endpoint returns an invoice: `GET /invoices/1041`. The code confirms the user is logged in and loads invoice 1041.

A user who is shown their own invoice at `/invoices/1041` tries `/invoices/1042`. If the server returns it, they can read every invoice in the system by counting.

This flaw is called an **insecure direct object reference** (IDOR). The request names an object directly, and the server never asks whether it belongs to the caller.

The fix is to check ownership on every access. The most reliable way is to make ownership part of the query itself.

```sql
-- flawed: any invoice, for anyone who is logged in
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1;

-- fixed: only this user's invoice
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2;
```

The second parameter comes from the session on the server, never from the request. An invoice that belongs to someone else is then simply not found.

steps.title: Random IDs are not a check
steps.text:
A common response is to replace `1042` with a long random identifier, so that the next one cannot be guessed. That helps. It does not fix the flaw.

Identifiers leak. They appear in links people share, in browser history, in logs, in emails and in the `Referer` header. Once someone has an identifier, an endpoint with no ownership check serves the record.

Unguessable IDs are a useful extra layer, and they stop an attacker from counting through every record. The authorization check is still required.

steps.title: Two directions
steps.text:
Access control fails in two directions, and both need checking.

**Horizontal.** A user reaches another user's data at the same level: someone else's invoice, messages or profile. This is the IDOR case.

**Vertical.** A user performs an action that needs a higher level: an ordinary user calls an administrator's endpoint. A typical cause is an admin page that is hidden from the menu and whose endpoints check nothing.

Hiding a button is not access control. The endpoint behind it is reachable by anyone who knows or guesses its address.

steps.title: The hidden page
steps.text: An application shows an "Admin" link in the menu only to administrators. The page it leads to, `/admin/users`, and the endpoint it calls, `POST /admin/users/delete`, check only that the caller is logged in.

steps.title: Check on the server, every time
steps.text:
Three rules prevent most of these flaws.

- **Enforce on the server.** Anything in the browser is advice to honest users.
- **Check every request.** Not only the page that leads to the action, and not only the first step of a multi-step flow. Each endpoint stands alone, since each can be called alone.
- **Check the specific object.** "May this user edit documents" is not enough. The question is "may this user edit this document".

A flow with several steps is a common trap. Step 1 checks permission and step 3 performs the action. An attacker calls step 3 directly.

steps.title: Deny by default
steps.text:
Structure the code so that forgetting a check results in no access.

The fragile design has each endpoint remember to call a check. A new endpoint written in a hurry has none, and is open to everyone.

The sturdy design turns it around. A central layer, such as middleware or a framework's policy system, refuses every request unless a rule explicitly allows it. A new endpoint with no rule is closed. The mistake then shows up as a feature that does not work, which is noticed at once, and not as an open door, which is not noticed at all.

Keep the rules in one place where you can. Authorization logic scattered through a hundred handlers cannot be reviewed.

steps.title: Roles and attributes
steps.text:
There are two common ways to express who may do what.

**Role-based access control** (RBAC) assigns users to roles such as `viewer`, `editor`, `admin`, and grants permissions to roles. It is simple to understand and to audit. It struggles when rules depend on the data: "editors may edit only documents in their own department".

**Attribute-based access control** (ABAC) decides from attributes of the user, the object and the context: the user's department, the document's owner, the time of day. It expresses fine-grained rules and is harder to reason about.

Most applications use roles for the broad strokes and add ownership checks for particular objects. Whichever model you use, the question is the same: can you say, for any user and any object, whether access is allowed, and can you test it?

steps.title: Least privilege
steps.text:
**Least privilege** means giving each user, service and credential only the access its job requires, and no more.

It applies beyond human users.

- **Service accounts.** The application's database account can read and write its own tables. It cannot drop them or read another service's data.
- **API keys.** A key for reading reports cannot issue refunds. Scope keys to one purpose.
- **Cloud roles.** A function that writes to one storage bucket has permission for that bucket, not for all storage.
- **People.** Engineers do not have standing administrator access to production. They request it for a task, for a limited time, and it is logged.

The benefit shows when something is compromised. A stolen credential can do only what that credential could do. This limit is called the **blast radius**. Least privilege keeps it small.

Access also accumulates. People change teams and keep their old permissions. Review access on a schedule and remove what is no longer needed.

steps.title: Multi-tenant systems
steps.text:
In a product that serves many customers from one database, each customer is a **tenant**. The most damaging authorization flaw there is one tenant seeing another's data.

Every query must be limited to the caller's tenant. Relying on every developer to add `WHERE tenant_id = ...` to every query will fail eventually. Stronger designs enforce it underneath the application code.

- A data-access layer that adds the tenant condition to every query automatically.
- **Row-level security** in the database: a rule on the table that hides rows of other tenants whatever query is run.
- For the most sensitive cases, a separate database or schema per tenant.

Test it directly. Create two tenants in a test, log in as one and try to read every kind of object that belongs to the other.

steps.title: Test the refusals
steps.text:
Functional tests check that allowed things work. Authorization flaws are things that should be refused and are not, so they need tests of their own.

For each endpoint, write tests that call it:

- with no login,
- as a user with too low a role,
- as a user of the right role who does not own the object,
- as a user of another tenant.

Each must be refused. These tests are dull to write, and they are the only automated protection against the most common serious flaw.

One detail on the response: for an object that exists and is not the caller's, returning `404 Not Found` in place of `403 Forbidden` avoids confirming that the object exists.

steps.title: The multi-step flow
steps.text: A refund takes three requests: `POST /refunds/start` checks that the caller is a manager and returns a refund ID. `POST /refunds/{id}/amount` sets the amount. `POST /refunds/{id}/confirm` pays it out. Only the first checks the role.

steps.title: Exercise: find the missing checks
steps.text:
A project management tool has organizations, projects inside them, and tasks inside projects. Users have a role per organization: `member` or `admin`. Review these endpoints. Each one checks only that the caller is logged in.

1. `GET /tasks/{task_id}` returns a task.
2. `PATCH /tasks/{task_id}` updates a task. The body may contain any task field, including `project_id`.
3. `GET /organizations/{org_id}/members` lists members with their email addresses.
4. `POST /organizations/{org_id}/members` adds a member. The body contains `user_id` and `role`.
5. `GET /export?org_id=...` returns all of an organization's data.
6. The front end hides the "Add member" button from non-admins.

Say what an attacker can do with each, and write the check each needs.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Read any task in any organization**, by trying IDs. Check: the task's project belongs to an organization the caller is a member of. Do it in the query, by joining tasks to projects to memberships with the caller's user ID.
2. **Change any task, and move it.** Beyond editing other organizations' tasks, setting `project_id` moves a task into or out of a project the caller has no right to. Check membership for the task's current project and for the target project, and accept only a listed set of fields.
3. **Collect every organization's member emails.** Check: the caller is a member of `org_id`.
4. **Join any organization as an admin.** A caller posts their own `user_id` with `role: admin`. Check: the caller is an admin of `org_id`. This is the most serious, since it grants full access to everything else.
5. **Download any organization's data.** Check: the caller is an admin of `org_id`. Take extra care here, since it is the most sensitive read: ask for the password again, rate limit it and log it.
6. **Nothing is protected by this.** It is fine as presentation. The check belongs on endpoint 4.

**The structural fix.** Six endpoints, six missing checks: the pattern is that each handler was meant to remember. Put a rule in front of every route: resolve the organization from the path or from the object, load the caller's role in it, and refuse unless the route's required role is met. A route with no declared rule is refused. Then add tests that call every endpoint as a member of a different organization.

lessons.title: Cryptography in practice
lessons.intro:
Developers rarely need to invent cryptography, and they often need to use it. This module covers the four tools, which one fits which job, and the mistakes that make correct algorithms useless.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: Four tools
steps.text:
Almost every use of cryptography in an application is one of four things.

| Tool | What it does | Key? | Reversible? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hashing | Produces a fixed-size fingerprint of data | No | No |
| Message authentication (MAC) | Proves data was made by someone who holds a key | One shared key | No |
| Encryption | Hides data from anyone without the key | One key, or a pair | Yes |
| Digital signature | Proves who made the data, checkable by anyone | A key pair | No |

Choosing the wrong one is the commonest mistake. People encrypt when they need a signature, or hash when they need a MAC. Start from the question: do I need to hide this, or to prove it has not been changed, or to prove who sent it?

steps.title: Hashing
steps.text:
A **hash function** turns data of any size into a short fixed-size value. The same input always gives the same output. Changing one bit of the input changes the output completely. There is no practical way to go backwards or to find two inputs with the same hash.

Use it for integrity: checking that a downloaded file is the file that was published, identifying content, detecting change.

SHA-256 and the SHA-3 family are current choices. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security purposes, since two different inputs with the same hash can be constructed, and should not be used for anything that an attacker might influence.

A plain hash has no key, so it proves nothing about who made it. Anyone can change the data and compute a new hash. And as the passwords module showed, a fast hash is the wrong tool for storing passwords.

steps.title: Message authentication
steps.text:
A **MAC** (message authentication code) is a fingerprint made from the data and a secret key together. Only someone who holds the key can produce the right value, and only someone who holds the key can check it. **HMAC** is the standard construction, as in HMAC-SHA-256.

Use it when the same party, or two parties who share a key, need to know that data was not changed in between.

- A webhook: the sender computes an HMAC of the body with a shared secret and puts it in a header. The receiver computes it again and compares. A forged or altered request does not match.
- A signed cookie or a token that the server gives to a client and later gets back.

Compare MAC values with a constant-time comparison, as with any secret.

steps.title: Symmetric encryption
steps.text:
**Symmetric encryption** uses one key to both encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and is what protects data in bulk: files, database fields, the contents of a TLS connection.

The current standard is **AES**. The algorithm alone is not the whole choice. It is used in a **mode**, and the mode matters a great deal.

Use an **authenticated encryption** mode, such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. It encrypts and also produces a tag that detects any change to the encrypted data. Without that, an attacker who cannot read the data may still be able to alter it in useful ways, and the decryption will not notice.

Each encryption also needs a **nonce** (also called an IV): a value that must be different every time the same key is used. Reusing a nonce with the same key can destroy the protection completely. A good library generates it for you.

steps.title: Asymmetric encryption and signatures
steps.text:
**Asymmetric cryptography** uses a pair of keys. The **public key** can be given to anyone. The **private key** is kept by its owner.

It solves two problems that a shared key cannot.

- **Encryption to someone you have never met.** Anyone can encrypt with the public key. Only the holder of the private key can decrypt.
- **Digital signatures.** The owner signs with the private key. Anyone can verify with the public key. A valid signature proves the data came from the holder of the private key and has not changed.

A signature differs from a MAC in who can check it. A MAC needs the secret key to verify, so anyone who can verify can also forge. A signature is verified with the public key, which cannot create signatures. That is why software updates, certificates and tokens checked by many services use signatures.

Asymmetric operations are slow, so in practice they are combined with symmetric ones. TLS uses the key pair to establish identity and agree on a fresh symmetric key, and then uses that key for the data.

steps.title: Which tool
steps.text: A payment provider sends your server a webhook that says "payment 8841 succeeded". You and the provider share a secret that was set up in advance. You need to be sure the message really came from the provider and was not altered.

steps.title: Do not write your own
steps.text:
The rule everyone repeats is true: do not design your own cryptography, and do not implement standard algorithms yourself.

The reasons are practical. A homemade scheme has been examined by one person. Standard ones have been attacked by experts for years. Even a correct algorithm implemented by hand tends to leak through timing, poor randomness or mishandled edge cases, none of which show up in tests, since a broken cipher still encrypts and decrypts.

The rule extends to combining pieces. Choosing a cipher, a mode, a padding and a MAC and wiring them together is designing a scheme.

So work at the highest level you can.

- Use TLS for data in transit, with the library's defaults.
- Use the storage encryption that your database or cloud platform provides.
- When you must encrypt in code, use a library that offers one "encrypt this with this key" function, which chooses sound primitives and handles the nonce.

steps.title: Randomness
steps.text:
Keys, tokens, session IDs, nonces and reset links all depend on values that cannot be predicted.

Ordinary random functions in programming languages are built for simulations and games. Their output looks random and can be predicted by someone who sees a few values. Using one for a session ID or a reset token makes those guessable.

Use the **cryptographically secure random generator** that your platform provides, which draws on the operating system. Every language has one, usually in a module with "secure", "secrets" or "crypto" in its name.

Never derive a secret from the time, a counter, a user ID or a hash of those. A hash of a predictable value is a predictable value.

steps.title: Keys are the hard part
steps.text:
A sound algorithm with a badly kept key protects nothing. Most real failures of encryption are failures of **key management**.

- **Keep keys apart from the data.** A key stored in the same database as the data it protects is taken in the same theft.
- **Never put keys in source code** or in a repository. The next module covers this.
- **Use a key management service** (KMS) or a secrets manager. The key stays inside the service, which performs operations with it and records every use.
- **Rotate keys.** Change them on a schedule and at once after any suspected leak. The design must allow that: store which key version encrypted each item.
- **Limit who and what can use each key**, and log every use.

A useful pattern is **envelope encryption**. Each item is encrypted with its own data key. The data key is encrypted with a master key that never leaves the KMS, and is stored beside the item. Rotating the master key then means re-encrypting small data keys, not all the data.

steps.title: In transit and at rest
steps.text:
Data needs protecting in two states.

**In transit**, moving over a network. Use TLS everywhere, including between your own services inside a private network. Do not disable certificate checking to make an error go away.

**At rest**, stored on a disk. Turn on the storage encryption of your database, disks, backups and object storage. It protects against a stolen disk or a mishandled backup.

Know the limit of encryption at rest. It is transparent to anything that reads through the database. An attacker who gets in through SQL injection, or with a stolen application credential, receives the data decrypted like any other reader. For the most sensitive fields, such as identity numbers, add encryption in the application, so that the database itself holds only encrypted values.

steps.title: Encoding is not encryption
steps.text:
Three things are often confused.

- **Encoding** (Base64, hex, URL encoding) changes how data is written. It needs no key and anyone can reverse it. It protects nothing.
- **Hashing** is one way and has no key.
- **Encryption** is reversible with a key.

A password stored as Base64 is stored in plain text. A JWT payload is Base64 and readable by anyone. If no key is needed to read a value, the value is not protected.

steps.title: Encrypted at rest
steps.text: A company's database is encrypted at rest with a key held in a key management service. An attacker exploits a SQL injection flaw in the web application and runs `SELECT * FROM customers`.

steps.title: Exercise: choose the tool
steps.text:
For each need, choose hashing, a MAC, symmetric encryption, a signature, or none of them, and say why. Name the specific pitfall to avoid.

1. Store users' national identity numbers so that support staff with database access cannot read them.
2. Let customers verify that a software update they downloaded really came from your company.
3. Produce a password reset token.
4. Make sure a "price" value that you send to the browser in a hidden field comes back unchanged.
5. Store API keys that you issue to customers.
6. "Protect" a user ID in a URL by Base64-encoding it.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Symmetric encryption in the application**, with an authenticated mode and a key in a KMS that the database and support staff cannot use. Storage encryption alone would not do it, since staff querying the database would see the values decrypted. Pitfall: keeping the key in the same database.
2. **A digital signature.** You sign each release with a private key, and customers verify with your public key. A MAC would require giving customers the secret, and then any customer could forge an update. Pitfall: the private signing key must be guarded more closely than almost anything else you hold.
3. **None of the four. It needs secure randomness.** Generate at least 128 random bits from the secure generator. Store a hash of the token and compare hashes. Pitfall: an ordinary random function, or a value derived from the time.
4. **A MAC**, if the value must travel through the browser. Better: do not send it at all. Keep the price on the server and look it up. Pitfall: believing that encrypting the field, or hiding it, prevents changes.
5. **A fast hash** (SHA-256) of each key, with the key shown to the customer once. The keys are long and random, so they cannot be guessed, and a slow password hash would only delay every API call. Pitfall: storing them in readable form, so that a database copy is a list of working keys.
6. **Nothing is protected.** Base64 is encoding. Anyone decodes it in a second. If the aim is to stop people reading other users' records, the answer is an authorization check on the server.

Half of these turn out to need no encryption. Deciding what the actual requirement is comes before choosing any algorithm.

lessons.title: Secrets
lessons.intro:
An application needs passwords, keys and tokens to reach its database and the services it calls. Each one is a way in for whoever holds it. This module covers where secrets leak, where they should live, and what to do when one gets out.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: What counts as a secret
steps.text:
A **secret** is any value that grants access by being known.

- Database passwords and connection strings.
- API keys and tokens for other services.
- Private keys: for TLS, for signing, for SSH.
- Encryption keys.
- Session signing keys and webhook secrets.
- Cloud credentials.

Non-secret configuration, such as a hostname, a port or a feature flag, needs no such care. The test is simple: if this value were posted publicly, could someone do harm with it?

steps.title: Where secrets leak
steps.text:
Secrets rarely leak through clever attacks. They leak through ordinary work.

- **Source code.** A key pasted into a file "for now" and committed.
- **Version history.** Deleted in a later commit and still present in every earlier one.
- **Configuration files** committed by mistake, such as a `.env` file.
- **Logs.** A request logged with its `Authorization` header. A connection string printed in an error.
- **Error pages and stack traces** shown to users.
- **Build systems.** Printed in pipeline output, or baked into a container image layer.
- **Front-end code.** Anything shipped to a browser or a mobile app can be extracted from it.
- **Chat, tickets, email and screenshots**, shared to "help debug".
- **Laptops and backups.**

Public code hosting sites are scanned continuously by automated tools. A cloud key pushed to a public repository is typically found and abused within minutes.

steps.title: Out of the code
steps.text:
The first rule is that a secret never appears in source code or in the repository, in any branch.

There are good reasons beyond leaks.

- Everyone with read access to the code, now and in the future, has the secret.
- The same secret ends up in development, testing and production, since the code is the same.
- Changing the secret needs a code change and a deploy.

The code should contain the name of the secret. The value is supplied when the application runs.

steps.title: Deleting is not removing
steps.text: A developer commits a file containing a live API key, notices ten minutes later, deletes the line and commits again. The repository is private and has 60 contributors.

steps.title: Where secrets should live
steps.text:
Supplying a value at run time can be done in several ways, from basic to strong.

**Environment variables.** The platform sets them when the process starts. They keep secrets out of the code, and every platform supports them. Their weaknesses: they are visible to anything running as the same user, they are often dumped in crash reports and debug pages, and there is no record of who read them.

**A secrets manager.** A dedicated service that stores secrets encrypted, hands them out to identities that are permitted, and records every access. Examples are Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager and HashiCorp Vault. This is the right home for production secrets.

A secrets manager gives you what environment variables cannot:

- **Access control** per secret: this service may read this one and no other.
- **An audit log** of every read.
- **Rotation**, often automatic.
- **One place** to change a value, with no redeploy.

steps.title: No secret at all
steps.text:
The best secret is one that does not exist. Many platforms let a workload prove its identity without holding any long-lived credential.

A service running in a cloud is given an identity by the platform itself, called a managed identity, a service account or a workload identity. When it calls the database or the storage service, the platform vouches for it with a short-lived token that it obtains and renews automatically. There is no password to store, leak or rotate.

The same idea applies to deployment pipelines. A pipeline can exchange a short-lived token from its own platform for temporary cloud access, with no stored cloud key. This is often called workload identity federation.

Prefer these wherever they are offered. Each one removes a secret from the system.

steps.title: Scope and separate
steps.text:
A leaked secret does as much damage as it has access. Limit that in advance.

- **One secret per service.** If ten services share one database password, a leak from any of them exposes all, and you cannot tell which leaked.
- **One set per environment.** Development, testing and production have different secrets. A developer's laptop never holds a production credential.
- **Least privilege.** A key for reading from one storage area cannot delete from another.
- **Short lifetimes.** A credential that expires in an hour is of little use to someone who finds it next week.

steps.title: Rotation
steps.text:
**Rotation** means replacing a secret with a new one and retiring the old.

Rotate on a schedule, so that a secret that leaked unnoticed stops working eventually. Rotate at once when a secret may have been exposed, and when someone with access to it leaves.

Rotation is only practical if it does not cause an outage, and that must be designed in.

1. Create the new secret while the old one still works.
2. Update the consumers to use the new one.
3. Confirm nothing uses the old one any more.
4. Revoke the old one.

Systems that accept two valid secrets at once for a short period make this painless. A secret that cannot be rotated without downtime will not be rotated, including on the day it leaks. Practise it before you need it.

steps.title: Secrets in the front end
steps.text:
Anything sent to a browser or packed into a mobile app is public. Minifying or obscuring the code does not change that. The values can be read from the network traffic or extracted from the app.

So a secret API key can never be used directly from front-end code. The pattern is to keep the key on your server and have the front end call your server, which adds the key and calls the third party.

Some keys are designed to be public, such as a map provider's browser key or a payment provider's "publishable" key. Those are identifiers, and they are protected by restrictions on the provider's side: which domains may use them and what they may do. Check which kind you have. If the provider's documentation says a key must be kept secret, it must not reach the browser.

steps.title: Keep them out of logs and pipelines
steps.text:
- **Logs.** Never log `Authorization` headers, cookies, connection strings or whole request bodies. Configure the logging library to mask known secret fields.
- **Error messages.** Show users a generic message. Keep details in the log.
- **Pipelines.** Use the pipeline's secret store, which masks values in output. Do not `echo` a secret to debug it. Do not pass secrets as command-line arguments, which appear in process lists.
- **Container images.** A secret copied in during a build stays in that image layer, even if a later step deletes the file. Supply secrets when the container runs, or use the build tool's secret mount feature.

steps.title: Catch them early
steps.text:
People make mistakes, so add checks that catch a secret before it spreads.

- **A pre-commit hook** that scans for patterns that look like keys and blocks the commit.
- **Scanning in the pipeline** and on the code hosting platform, across the whole history.
- **A `.gitignore` entry** for local configuration files, in place from the first commit.

Scanners match known formats, so they miss secrets that have no recognisable shape. They are a safety net, and the habit of never typing a secret into a file is still the main defence.

steps.title: When a secret leaks
steps.text:
A leaked secret is an incident. The order of the steps matters.

1. **Revoke it at once.** Make the leaked value useless. This is the only step that actually stops misuse. Do it first, even if it breaks something.
2. **Issue a new secret** and deploy it.
3. **Check for misuse.** Read the access logs of whatever the secret protected, from the time of the leak.
4. **Remove it from where it leaked**, as tidying. This does not make the old value safe, which is why it comes after revocation.
5. **Find out how it happened** and close that path.

The common mistake is to do step 4 first and stop: deleting the commit and hoping nobody saw it. Assume it was seen.

steps.title: The key in the app
steps.text: A mobile app includes a secret API key for a paid text-messaging service, so that the app can send verification messages directly. The key is stored obfuscated in the app's code.

steps.title: Exercise: clean up the secrets
steps.text:
A team's service is set up as follows.

1. `app.config` in the repository contains the production database password and a payment provider's secret key.
2. The same database password is used by five services and by the developers for local debugging against production.
3. The pipeline prints its environment at the start of every run, "to help with debugging". The logs are kept for 90 days.
4. The Dockerfile copies a `.env` file into the image and deletes it in the next step.
5. Nobody knows how to change the payment key without downtime, so it has not been changed in four years. Two engineers who knew it have left.

Write a plan. Put the steps in order and say what each one achieves.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**1. Treat every one of these secrets as leaked, and rotate them.** They are in the repository history, in 90 days of pipeline logs and in image layers, and former staff know them. Nothing done to the files makes the current values safe. Start with the payment key, since it handles money, and work out the two-key rotation with the provider so that there is no downtime.

**2. Move secrets to a secrets manager.** Each service reads its own secrets at start-up, under its own identity. `app.config` keeps only the names. This is what makes the rotation in step 1 repeatable.

**3. Give each service its own database account**, with only the rights it needs. Where the platform supports it, replace the password with a managed identity. Developers get no production credentials on their machines. Debugging against production goes through a logged, time-limited access process.

**4. Stop the leaks at their sources.**

- Remove the environment dump from the pipeline, and use its masked secret store.
- Fix the Dockerfile. The `.env` file is still inside the earlier layer. Supply configuration when the container runs.
- Add secret scanning as a pre-commit hook and in the pipeline, and add `.env` to `.gitignore`.

**5. Make rotation routine.** Put it on a schedule, and add "rotate shared secrets" to the checklist for when someone leaves.

**6. Review the access logs** of the database and the payment account for use that cannot be explained.

The order matters. Cleaning the repository first would feel productive and would leave four-year-old credentials working. Revoking is what removes the risk.

questions.prompt: Is the key safe now?

choices.text: Yes, since the line is gone
choices.feedback: The current version no longer has it. Every earlier version does.

choices.text: No. It is still in the history, and in every clone made in those ten minutes
choices.feedback: A version control system keeps every commit. The only safe response is to treat the key as leaked: revoke it and issue a new one.

choices.text: Yes, since the repository is private
choices.feedback: Private limits who can read it. Sixty people, their laptops and any tool with repository access can.

questions.prompt: What is the exposure?

choices.text: Little, since the key is obfuscated
choices.feedback: Obfuscation slows a reader down. The app has to turn it back into the real key to use it, and that can be observed.

choices.text: Anyone can extract the key from the app, or from its network traffic, and send messages at the company's cost
choices.feedback: Everything shipped to a device is in the user's hands. The app should ask the company's own server, which holds the key and decides whether to send.

choices.text: None, since app stores check apps for security
choices.feedback: Store review does not prevent a key from being extracted from a published app.

lessons.title: Dependencies and the supply chain
lessons.intro:
Most of the code in an application was written by someone else. This module covers the risks that come with that, how to keep third-party code current, and how to protect the path from source code to running software.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy.

steps.title: Most of your code is not yours
steps.text:
A typical application's own code is a small fraction of what runs. The rest is libraries, their libraries, a language runtime, a base container image and an operating system.

A package you install is a **direct dependency**. The packages it needs in turn are **transitive dependencies**. A project that lists 40 packages commonly installs over a thousand.

Every one of them runs with the full rights of your application. It can read your environment, your files and your secrets, and it can make network requests. Installing a package means trusting its authors, and the authors of everything it depends on, with all of that.

steps.title: Known vulnerabilities
steps.text:
Flaws are found in libraries constantly. When one is published, it gets an identifier, a **CVE** number, and usually a fixed version is released.

From that moment the flaw is public knowledge. Attackers scan the internet for applications still running the old version. Many large breaches used a flaw whose fix had been available for weeks or months and had not been applied.

So the first job is to know when something you use has a known flaw.

- **Dependency scanners** compare the versions you have installed against databases of known vulnerabilities and report matches. Most ecosystems have one built in or freely available, and code hosting platforms run them automatically.
- **Run them in the pipeline** on every build, and on a schedule, since a new flaw can be published for code that has not changed.

A scanner produces noise. Not every finding matters to you: the vulnerable function may never be called, or the package may be used only in development. Judge findings by severity and by whether the flaw is reachable, and have a clear rule for how fast each level must be fixed.

steps.title: Keep up to date
steps.text:
The surest way to be able to apply a security fix quickly is to already be on a recent version. A project that is three major versions behind cannot take a one-line patch. It first faces weeks of upgrade work, during which the flaw stays open.

- **Update routinely and in small steps.** Frequent small updates are low-risk. A large jump once every two years is a project.
- **Automate the proposals.** Tools such as Dependabot and Renovate open a change for each available update, which your tests then check.
- **Have good tests.** Automated updates are only as safe as the tests that run on them.
- **Watch for end of life.** A version of a language or framework that is no longer supported receives no security fixes at all. Plan upgrades before that date.

steps.title: Pin what you install
steps.text:
A dependency declaration such as "version 2.x" means the exact version is chosen at install time. Two builds of the same commit can then contain different code.

A **lock file** records the exact version of every package, direct and transitive, together with a hash of its contents. Installing from it gives the same code every time.

- **Commit the lock file.**
- **Install from it in the pipeline**, with the command that fails if the lock file and the declaration disagree.
- **Review changes to it.** A lock file change is a code change. It is where a new package or a new version enters.

Pinning does not mean never updating. It means updates happen as a visible, reviewed change, and not silently at build time.

steps.title: The unpinned build
steps.text: A project declares its dependencies with version ranges and has no lock file. Its pipeline installs the latest matching versions on every build. On Tuesday, the maintainer account of a small transitive dependency is taken over, and a harmful version is published. The project's nightly build runs.

steps.title: Malicious packages
steps.text:
Not every bad package is an accident. Attackers publish harmful code on purpose.

- **Typosquatting.** A package with a name one keystroke from a popular one, waiting for a mistyped install command.
- **Dependency confusion.** A public package with the same name as a company's private one. A misconfigured installer prefers the public one.
- **Account takeover.** A legitimate maintainer's account is compromised and a harmful version is published under the trusted name.
- **A handover.** An abandoned package is given to a new maintainer, who adds harmful code.

Defences:

- Check the exact name before installing, especially when copying from a tutorial or a generated suggestion.
- Configure private package names so that they resolve only from your private registry.
- Use lock files with hashes.
- Be cautious with install scripts, which run code at install time.
- Be slower to adopt a version that was published in the last few hours.

steps.title: Choosing a dependency
steps.text:
Every dependency is a long-term commitment. Before adding one, ask:

- **Do we need it?** A package for a ten-line function adds its whole dependency tree and all future maintenance.
- **Is it maintained?** Look at recent releases, the response to reported issues and the number of maintainers.
- **How widely is it used?** Wide use means more people who would notice a problem.
- **How large is its own tree?**
- **Does it have a way to report security issues**, and a history of fixing them?

Fewer dependencies is a security property. Each one removed is code you no longer have to trust or update.

steps.title: Know what you ship
steps.text:
When a serious flaw is announced in a common library, the first question is "are we affected, and where?". Many organizations cannot answer it quickly.

A **software bill of materials** (SBOM) is a list of every component in a piece of software, with versions. Generated at build time and stored for each release, it turns that question into a search.

Base images and system packages belong on the list as well. A container image contains an operating system's worth of packages, and a flaw in one of those is as real as a flaw in an application library. Rebuild images regularly to pick up fixes, and prefer small base images, which contain less.

steps.title: The pipeline is production
steps.text:
Whatever can change the build can change what runs. The build and deployment pipeline therefore deserves the same protection as the production system.

- **Protect the main branch.** Require review before merging. No direct pushes.
- **Limit who can change the pipeline definition**, and review those changes.
- **Give the pipeline least privilege.** A job that runs tests needs no deploy credentials. Use short-lived credentials where the platform offers them.
- **Do not run untrusted code with secrets.** A build triggered by an outside contributor's change must not have access to deployment secrets.
- **Pin third-party pipeline steps** to an exact version, preferably by commit hash. A reusable step from someone else's repository is a dependency like any other, and one that runs with your secrets.
- **Build once, and deploy that same artefact** everywhere, so that what was tested is what runs.

steps.title: Verify what you run
steps.text:
Two further practices raise the level for systems that need it.

- **Signing.** The build signs each artefact, and the deployment refuses anything without a valid signature. An artefact that was swapped or altered after the build is rejected.
- **Provenance.** A signed record of how an artefact was built: from which commit, by which pipeline. It lets you check that what you run was made from the code you reviewed.

These add work, and they belong after the basics: scanning, lock files, updates and a protected pipeline.

steps.title: Code you did not write still needs review
steps.text:
Third-party code enters in other ways than a package manager.

- A snippet copied from a forum answer.
- Code produced by an AI assistant.
- A script piped straight from a URL into a shell.

Read it before running it, and review it as you would a colleague's change. Generated code can contain the flaws from earlier modules, and can suggest a package name that does not exist, which an attacker may later register. Check that every package it names is real and is the one you intend.

steps.title: The pipeline step
steps.text: A deployment workflow uses a third-party step from a public repository, referenced by a moving tag, `v2`. The step receives the cloud deployment credentials. The step's repository is compromised and the `v2` tag is moved to a new commit.

steps.title: Exercise: assess the project
steps.text:
You join a team and find this.

1. 62 direct dependencies. The scanner, run for the first time, reports 140 findings: 3 critical, 21 high and the rest lower.
2. No lock file. The pipeline installs the latest versions.
3. The language runtime reached end of life 14 months ago.
4. The base image is `latest` of a full operating system image, rebuilt "when someone remembers".
5. The pipeline uses nine third-party steps, all referenced by a major version tag, and every job has the production deploy key.
6. Six of the dependencies have had no release in five years.

Put the work in order, with a reason for each position.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**1. Triage the 3 critical findings today.** For each, ask whether the vulnerable code is reachable in this application and whether it faces the internet. Patch the ones that are. This is the only item that may be an open door at this moment.

**2. Add a lock file and make the pipeline install from it.** It takes an afternoon, it stops silent changes, and it makes every later step reproducible. Commit it before upgrading anything, so there is a known starting point.

**3. Fix the pipeline's privileges.** Give the deploy key only to the deploy job. Pin the nine third-party steps to commit hashes. This is cheap, and it closes the path with the highest impact, since that key can change production.

**4. Work through the 21 high findings**, then set a rule: critical within days, high within weeks. Turn on automated update proposals so the backlog does not return.

**5. Plan the runtime upgrade.** Fourteen months without security fixes is a growing risk. It is also the largest piece of work, so it needs scheduling. Some findings will disappear with it.

**6. Pin and slim the base image.** Use a specific, small image, and rebuild it on a schedule.

**7. Review the six abandoned dependencies.** Replace or remove them. With 62 direct dependencies, some can probably go altogether.

**8. Generate an SBOM per release**, so that the next urgent question can be answered by searching.

The order puts possible live exposure first, then cheap changes that prevent new problems, then the large upgrade. Fixing all 140 findings in list order would have delayed the three things that matter most.

questions.prompt: What happens?

choices.text: Nothing, since nobody changed the project's code
choices.feedback: The code did not change. What the build installs did.

choices.text: The harmful version is installed and shipped, with no change anyone could review
choices.feedback: Without a lock file, each build takes whatever is newest. A lock file would have kept the previous version until someone chose to update.

choices.text: The package registry blocks harmful packages
choices.feedback: Registries remove them once reported, which is often days later.

questions.prompt: What happens on the next run?

choices.text: The run fails, since the code behind the tag changed
choices.feedback: Nothing checks that. A tag is a label that can be moved.

choices.text: The new code runs with the deployment credentials, and can send them anywhere
choices.feedback: A moving tag means "whatever the owner points it at today". Pinning the step to a full commit hash would have kept the reviewed version.

choices.text: Nothing, since third-party steps run in a sandbox
choices.feedback: The step was handed the credentials on purpose. It can use them.

lessons.title: Protect personal and sensitive data
lessons.intro:
Data that was never collected cannot leak. This module covers how to decide what data deserves which care, how to hold less of it, and the places where sensitive data ends up without anyone having chosen to put it there.

The advice here is general guidance, not any organization's policy. It is not legal advice. Privacy law differs by country and sector, and the rules that apply to a real system must come from the people responsible for compliance where you work.

steps.title: Not all data is equal
steps.text:
Protecting everything to the highest standard is too expensive, and protecting everything to the lowest is negligent. The first step is **classification**: sorting data by how much harm its exposure would cause.

A simple scheme has four levels.

| Level | Examples | Typical handling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public | Marketing pages, published prices | No restriction |
| Internal | Internal documentation, non-sensitive metrics | Staff only |
| Confidential | Customer names, emails, order history | Need-to-know access, encrypted, logged |
| Restricted | Passwords, payment card data, health records, identity numbers | Strictest controls, minimal access, often regulated |

The exact names matter less than having them, writing down which data is at which level, and having rules for each level that people can follow.

steps.title: Personal data
steps.text:
**Personal data** (also called PII, for personally identifiable information) is any information about an identifiable person. It is broader than most people assume.

- **Direct identifiers:** name, email address, phone number, identity number.
- **Indirect identifiers:** an IP address, a device ID, a precise location, an account number.
- **Combinations.** A postcode, a date of birth and a gender are each harmless and together identify most individuals.

Some kinds are treated as especially sensitive in most privacy laws, since exposure can cause serious harm: health data, biometric data, financial details, and information about beliefs, origin or private life.

Removing the name from a record does not make it anonymous. If the remaining fields can be linked back to a person, it is still personal data.

steps.title: Collect less
steps.text:
The most reliable protection is not to have the data. This is **data minimisation**.

- **Ask for what the feature needs.** A newsletter sign-up needs an email address. It does not need a date of birth.
- **Question every field** in a form and every column in a table: what is this used for? If nobody can say, do not collect it.
- **Prefer a less precise form.** An age range in place of a date of birth. A city in place of an address. The last four digits of a card in place of the number.
- **Do not copy production data** into development and test environments. Those are far less protected. Use generated data, or data with the identifying fields replaced.

Every field you hold is a field to secure, to include in a breach notice, and to produce or delete when a person asks for their data.

steps.title: Keep it for less time
steps.text:
Data kept for ever is exposed for ever. **Retention** means deciding how long each kind of data is needed and removing it afterwards.

- Set a period per kind of data, based on why it is held: account data while the account exists, logs for some months, financial records for as long as the law requires.
- Delete or anonymise automatically, on a schedule. A manual process does not happen.
- Remember the copies: backups, exports, analytics stores, caches, search indexes and the systems of third parties you sent the data to.

A breach of a system with a 90-day retention rule exposes 90 days of data. The same breach without one exposes ten years.

steps.title: The breach that was smaller
steps.text: Two companies suffer the same breach of their order databases. Company A keeps every order since it started, with full card numbers and dates of birth "in case they are useful". Company B keeps the last four card digits, no dates of birth, and removes personal details from orders older than two years.

steps.title: Where sensitive data hides
steps.text:
Sensitive data spreads to places nobody designed for it. Most accidental exposure comes from these.

- **Logs.** Request bodies, query strings, headers and error messages often contain personal data, tokens and passwords. Logs are widely readable, kept for a long time and frequently sent to outside services.
- **URLs.** Anything in a query string is recorded in browser history, server logs and proxy logs, and is sent to other sites in the `Referer` header.
- **Error messages and debug pages.**
- **Analytics and tracking tools,** which receive page addresses and form values.
- **Emails and notifications.**
- **Exports and spreadsheets** on laptops and shared drives.
- **Backups,** which hold everything and are often protected less than the database.
- **Caches and search indexes.**
- **Support tools and screenshots.**

When you handle a sensitive field, follow it through the system and list every place it is written.

steps.title: Log without leaking
steps.text:
Logs are necessary, and they are the most common unplanned store of sensitive data.

- **Log identifiers, not contents.** `user_id=5521 updated profile` and not the new profile.
- **Never log** passwords, tokens, session IDs, card numbers, identity numbers or full request bodies.
- **Mask by default.** Configure the logging library to redact fields with known names, such as `password`, `token`, `authorization`, `card`.
- **Keep personal data out of URLs,** so it does not land in access logs.
- **Treat logs as sensitive data** themselves: limit who can read them, and set a retention period.

steps.title: Mask, tokenise, pseudonymise
steps.text:
When data must be kept, reduce how many places hold the real value.

- **Masking** shows part of a value: `**** **** **** 4242`. Support staff can confirm a card with a customer without ever seeing the number.
- **Tokenisation** replaces a sensitive value with a meaningless stand-in, the token. The real value is kept in one tightly guarded vault. Every other system stores and passes around the token. Payment processing commonly works this way: your system holds a token and the payment provider holds the card.
- **Pseudonymisation** replaces identifiers with artificial ones, so that records can still be linked to each other and no longer directly to a person. The mapping is kept separately. It lowers risk. The data is still personal, since the mapping exists.
- **Anonymisation** removes the link to a person permanently. It is much harder to achieve than it sounds, since combinations of ordinary fields can identify people again.

The greatest gain is often to keep the most sensitive data out of your system altogether. If a specialist provider holds the card numbers, your own breach cannot expose them.

steps.title: Control and record access
steps.text:
For confidential and restricted data, who can read it matters as much as how it is stored.

- **Need to know.** Access is granted for a role's actual tasks. Most engineers do not need to read customer records.
- **Access is logged.** Record who viewed which sensitive record and when. Logging reads, and not only changes, is what makes misuse by insiders detectable.
- **Bulk access is special.** Reading one customer's record is routine. Exporting 100,000 is not. Limit it, require approval and alert on it.
- **Show less.** Internal tools should mask sensitive fields by default, with a deliberate, logged action to reveal one.

steps.title: People's rights over their data
steps.text:
Many privacy laws give people rights over data about them, such as the GDPR in Europe. The details vary. The common ones affect system design.

- **Access.** A person may ask what you hold about them and receive a copy.
- **Correction.** They may ask for wrong data to be fixed.
- **Deletion.** They may ask for their data to be erased, within limits.
- **Purpose limitation.** Data collected for one purpose should not be quietly used for another.

These are far easier to honour when planned for. Know where each person's data lives, across every store and every third party, and be able to find it by one identifier. A system with personal data scattered through twenty tables and five vendors, and no map of it, cannot answer a deletion request with confidence.

steps.title: Third parties
steps.text:
Every outside service that receives your data extends your attack surface to theirs: analytics, error tracking, email delivery, support desks, AI services.

- Send each one the minimum it needs. An error tracker does not need request bodies.
- Know which services hold what, and keep the list current.
- Check what a service does with the data, where it stores it and how long it keeps it.
- Remove integrations that are no longer used. Each was given data and usually a credential.

steps.title: The query string
steps.text: A password reset page is reached by a link such as `https://app.example.com/reset?email=ana@example.com&token=k3Xp9aTq8w`. The page loads a script from an analytics provider.

steps.title: Exercise: follow the data
steps.text:
A telehealth product lets patients book video appointments. A booking stores: full name, date of birth, email, phone, a free-text "reason for visit", an insurance number and a payment card. The team reports:

1. The application logs every request body at debug level, and debug logging is on in production.
2. The test environment is refreshed weekly from a copy of the production database.
3. The support tool shows all fields of a booking to all 80 support agents.
4. Bookings are never deleted.
5. An error tracking service receives the full request and response for every error.
6. The card number is stored in the bookings table.

Classify the data. Then say what you would change for each of the six, and name the one you would do first.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Classification.** The reason for visit is health data, and the insurance number and card number are highly sensitive: all three are restricted. Name, date of birth, email and phone are confidential, and here they are tied to a medical service, which raises their sensitivity.

**Changes**

1. **Logs.** Turn off body logging in production. Log identifiers and outcomes only, mask known sensitive fields, and treat the existing logs as holding health and card data: restrict them and shorten their retention.
2. **Test data.** Stop copying production. Use generated data. Until then, the test environment holds real patients' health data with test-level protection.
3. **Support tool.** Show what the task needs: name, appointment time and status. Mask the insurance number and the reason for visit, with a logged "reveal" for the cases that need it. Limit who can reveal.
4. **Retention.** Set periods with the compliance owner. Medical and financial records often have minimum periods by law, so the answer is not simply "delete". Remove what is not required once the period ends.
5. **Error tracker.** Strip bodies and personal fields before sending. Send an error type, a stack trace and an internal ID.
6. **Card numbers.** Stop storing them. Use the payment provider's tokenisation, so the bookings table holds a token and the last four digits.

**First: item 6, then item 1.** Stored card numbers are the highest-impact data here and the easiest to stop holding. Body logging comes next, since it copies every restricted field, the card number included, into a second, widely readable store.

These are engineering suggestions. For a real product of this kind, the retention periods, the handling of health data and the response to what the logs already contain are decisions for the people responsible for compliance and security.

choices.feedback: HTTPS protects the address in transit. It does nothing about where each end records it.
